Sampling Interventional Distributions with Orthogonal MMD Flow

Bariscan Bozkurt Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London    Hugh Dance Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London    Zonghao Chen Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London    Alexandre Galashov Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London    Arthur Gretton Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London    Houssam Zenati Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London
Abstract

Many causal inference problems require sampling from interventional outcome distributions rather than estimating low-dimensional summaries. Existing approaches often rely on fitting generative models of the target distribution together with additional nuisance components, which can be computationally demanding for high-dimensional outcomes. We propose Interventional Maximum Mean Discrepancy Flow (IMMD-Flow), a particle-based method that instead represents the target interventional distribution through its kernel mean embedding. This kernel embedding admits a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal estimator with finite-sample guarantees and can be efficiently reused to sample from the interventional distribution via MMD gradient flow. IMMD-Flow accommodates both hard and soft interventions, admits theoretical guarantees for estimation and particle approximation, and extends to high-dimensional image outcomes through frozen encoders. Across image-based benchmarks, IMMD-Flow matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative approaches while showing significant speed advantages.

1 Introduction

Interventional sampling aims to generate outcomes from the distribution induced by a specified intervention rather than from the observational distribution. This is particularly useful for high-dimensional outcomes. For example, one may wish to generate images with a given demographic attribute AA while adjusting contextual features, such as clothing or background, so that their distribution does not inherit spurious associations with AA from the observational data. Such tasks arise in representational fairness and bias mitigation [61, 13, 7].

Recent approaches construct interventional samplers by specifying a parameterized generative or density-based model, identifying from observational data a training objective that targets the interventional law, and optimizing this objective over the model parameters [30, 43, 40, 39, 15]. This yields flexible samplers, but requires first learning a generative model in addition to the nuisance functions required for causal adjustment. While recent work has simplified the generative learning problem via using flows from data-adaptive source distributions [15], we show the computational cost remains burdensome.

In this work, we introduce Interventional MMD Flow (IMMD-Flow), a method for sampling from interventional distributions which bypasses the need to first learn an explicit generative model. The central idea is to formulate interventional sampling as a sample-based distributional optimization problem, in which an empirical distribution of particles is directly optimized to match the target distribution. We instantiate this using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), for which the target distribution enters the objective only through its kernel mean embedding [21, 58]. Thus, once the interventional kernel mean embedding is estimated from observational data, samples can be generated directly by evolving the particles under the corresponding MMD gradient flow [2].

The remaining difficulty is statistical: neither the interventional embedding nor samples from the interventional distribution are observed. Under standard identification assumptions, the embedding can be represented through either the treatment-assignment mechanism or a conditional outcome embedding [45, 62]. However, each representation alone is sensitive to nuisance misspecification. We therefore combine them through a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal estimator [3, 10, 19]. This estimator has a simple closed form, can be computed efficiently using a projected Nyström approximation, and has bias of product order in the two nuisance errors. Since the target-dependent component of the squared MMD is linear in the interventional embedding, this second-order robustness carries directly over to the sampling objective. For smooth kernels, the same estimation error also controls perturbations of the induced transport velocity.

Our main contributions are as follows: (i) we formulate interventional sampling as MMD-based distributional optimization and derive a doubly robust, Neyman-orthogonal fixed target whose estimation error perturbs the transport velocity only at product order; (ii) we develop IMMD-Flow and a projected Nyström implementation that reduces conditional embedding regression costs and enables reuse across supported interventions; (iii) for smooth kernels, we derive finite-particle guarantees that propagate target-estimation error through the flow without requiring the estimated target to be a probability embedding, yielding conditions for convergence to the true interventional law; and (iv) we evaluate sampling accuracy, nuisance robustness, and computational performance on synthetic and structured-outcome benchmarks.

Section 2 defines the sampling problem, Section 3 develops IMMD-Flow, Section 4 gives the practical procedure, and Section 5 provides the statistical and particle-level analysis, and Section  6 empirically evaluate our method on several benchmarks. We provide a more detailed discussion of related work in Appendix A.

2 Problem Statement

We study the problem of generating outcomes under a known soft intervention from observational data. We first identify the interventional outcome law and then formulate sampling from this law as optimization over probability measures.

Interventional target and identification. Let 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, and 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} be Polish spaces, and write 𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Y}}) for the set of probability measures on 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}. Let O=(X,A,Y)∼P0O=(X,A,Y)\sim P_{0}, where XX, AA, and YY denote pretreatment covariates, treatment, and outcome, and

P0​(d​y,d​a,d​x)=PY|A,X​(d​y|a,x)​π0​(d​a|x)​PX​(d​x)P_{0}(dy,da,dx)=P_{Y\mid A,X}(dy|a,x)\,\pi_{0}(da|x)\,P_{X}(dx) (1)

where PXP_{X} is the marginal law of XX, π0(⋅∣x):=P0(A∈⋅∣X=x)\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x):=P_{0}(A\in\cdot\mid X=x) is the observational assignment mechanism, and PY|A,XP_{Y\mid A,X} is the conditional outcome law.

Let {Y⁡(a):a∈𝒜}\{Y(a):a\in{\mathcal{A}}\} be a jointly measurable potential-outcome process [52, 50]. A fixed, known soft intervention π\pi is a Markov kernel x↦π(⋅∣x)x\mapsto\pi(\cdot\mid x) from 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} [48, 46]. Its interventional outcome law Pπ∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)P^{\pi}\in\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Y}}) is defined by

Pπ(B)=𝔼[∫𝒜𝟏{Y(a)∈B}π(da∣X)],P^{\pi}(B)=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\mathbf{1}\{Y(a)\in B\}\,\pi(da\mid X)\right], (2)

where B⊆𝒴​ is Borel measurableB\subseteq{\mathcal{Y}}\ \text{ is Borel measurable}. Thus, PπP^{\pi} is the outcome law induced by replacing the observational assignment mechanism π0\pi_{0} with the intervention π\pi.

Assumption 2.1 (Identification).

The following standard conditions hold [50, 48, 46]:

  1. 1.

    Consistency: Y=Y⁡(A)Y=Y(A) almost surely.

  2. 2.

    Conditional exchangeability: {Y⁡(a)}a∈𝒜⟂A|X\{Y(a)\}_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}\perp A\mid X.

  3. 3.

    Overlap: π(⋅∣x)≪π0(⋅∣x)\pi(\cdot\mid x)\ll\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x) for PXP_{X}-almost every xx.

Proposition 2.2 (Identification of the interventional law).

Under Assumption 2.1, PπP^{\pi} is identified from P0P_{0}. For every measurable B⊆𝒴B\subseteq{\mathcal{Y}},

Pπ​(B)=∫𝒳∫𝒜PY|A,X​(B|a,x)​π​(𝑑a|x)​PX​(𝑑x).P^{\pi}(B)=\int_{{\mathcal{X}}}\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}P_{Y|A,X}(B|a,x)\,\pi(da|x)\,P_{X}(dx). (3)

Since PY|A,XP_{Y\mid A,X} is defined only PX​(d​x)​π0​(d​a∣x)P_{X}(dx)\pi_{0}(da\mid x)-almost everywhere, overlap ensures that Equation 3 is invariant to its choice of version. Hence PπP^{\pi} is a well-defined functional of P0P_{0} and π\pi.

Interventional sampling as distributional optimization. Sampling from Pπ∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)P^{\pi}\in\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Y}}) means generating a random outcome Y~∈𝒴\widetilde{Y}\in{\mathcal{Y}} such that

Pr⁡(Y~∈B)=Pπ​(B),B⊆𝒴​measurable.\Pr(\widetilde{Y}\in B)=P^{\pi}(B),\qquad B\subseteq{\mathcal{Y}}\ \text{measurable}. (4)

Our goal is therefore to generate from the full interventional outcome distribution, rather than to estimate a particular functional of it.

Although Proposition 2.2 identifies PπP^{\pi}, direct samples from it are unavailable: the observed outcomes arise under π0\pi_{0}, rather than under the intervention π\pi. Transport-based sampling provides a constructive alternative by progressively transforming samples from a tractable reference distribution toward the target [41, 1]. This can be formalized as optimization over probability measures. The resulting formulation can be called sampling distributional optimization (SDO): choose a functional ℱπ:𝒫⁡(𝒴)→ℝ∪{+∞}\mathcal{F}_{\pi}:\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Y}})\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} whose minimizer is the interventional law,

Pπ∈arg​minQ∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)⁡ℱπ​(Q),P^{\pi}\in\argmin_{Q\in\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Y}})}\mathcal{F}_{\pi}(Q), (SDO)

and construct dynamics that decrease ℱπ\mathcal{F}_{\pi} from a distribution that can be sampled directly [28, 1].

Let Q0∈𝒫⁡(𝒴)Q_{0}\in\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Y}}) denote such a reference distribution and (Qt)t≥0(Q_{t})_{t\geq 0} the laws induced by the resulting dynamics. If the objective converges to its minimum and ℱπ\mathcal{F}_{\pi} controls convergence of probability measures, then Qt⇒Pπ​as ​t→∞.Q_{t}\Rightarrow P^{\pi}\kern 5.0pt\text{as }t\to\infty. Hence, if Y~t∼Qt\widetilde{Y}_{t}\sim Q_{t}, the evolved outputs become asymptotically distributed according to PπP^{\pi}. Wasserstein gradient flows provide a principled way to construct such measure-valued dynamics, while particle approximations yield practical sampling algorithms [1, 34, 2].

The choice of ℱπ\mathcal{F}_{\pi} is therefore central: it must identify the interventional target while remaining amenable to estimation and transport without direct samples from PπP^{\pi}. In the next section, we show that maximum mean discrepancy has this structure. Its dependence on PπP^{\pi} reduces to a kernel mean embedding, which admits an orthogonal representation under the observational law and induces the transport dynamics used for sampling.

3 Interventional MMD Flow

The sampling distributional optimization formulation in equation SDO formulation requires a distributional objective that identifies the interventional target and is estimable from observational data. We use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) [21, 58], whose target dependence is linear in a kernel mean embedding. This structure permits an orthogonal observed-data representation [10, 19] and, subsequently, explicit transport dynamics [2, 25, 20, 9].

3.1 MMD objective for interventional sampling

To define the spatial dynamics used below, we work on 𝒵=ℝdZ{\mathcal{Z}}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{Z}}. Fix a measurable representation map E:𝒴→𝒵E:{\mathcal{Y}}\to{\mathcal{Z}} and write Z:=E⁡(Y),Qπ:=E#​Pπ,Z:=E(Y),\kern 5.0ptQ^{\pi}:=E_{\#}P^{\pi}, where E#​PπE_{\#}P^{\pi} is the pushforward of PπP^{\pi} through EE. When 𝒴=ℝdZ{\mathcal{Y}}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{Z}}, taking E=IdE=\mathrm{Id} recovers the outcome-space construction; otherwise, EE provides a latent space representation. The flow targets QπQ^{\pi}, and recovery of PπP^{\pi} after decoding is treated separately. Both the representation and the kernel below are fixed throughout this section.

Let k:𝒵×𝒵→ℝk:{\mathcal{Z}}\times{\mathcal{Z}}\to\mathbb{R} be a bounded, continuous, positive-definite, characteristic kernel, with reproducing kernel Hilbert space ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and feature map φ⁡(z):=k⁡(z,⋅)\varphi(z):=k(z,\cdot). Boundedness ensures that, for every Q∈𝒫⁡(𝒵)Q\in\mathcal{P}({\mathcal{Z}}), μQ:=∫𝒵φ⁡(z)​Q​(𝑑z),χ⁡(π):=μQπ\mu_{Q}:=\int_{{\mathcal{Z}}}\varphi(z)\,Q(dz),\kern 5.0pt\chi(\pi):=\mu_{Q^{\pi}} are well-defined elements of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. The latter is the interventional mean embedding, following the representation of causal distributions by Muandet et al. [45], Zenati et al. [62]. We take the sampling objective to be

ℱπ​(Q):=12​‖μQ−χ⁡(π)‖ℋ2=12​MMDk2⁡(Q,Qπ).\mathcal{F}_{\pi}(Q):=\frac{1}{2}\|\mu_{Q}-\chi(\pi)\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{MMD}_{k}^{2}(Q,Q^{\pi}). (5)

Characteristicness gives ℱπ​(Q)=0\mathcal{F}_{\pi}(Q)=0 if and only if Q=QπQ=Q^{\pi}. For weak-consistency conclusions, we additionally require that MMDk\operatorname{MMD}_{k} metrizes weak convergence; under this condition, vanishing objective values imply weak convergence to QπQ^{\pi} [55].

For observational estimation, the useful feature of Equation 5 is its risk representation. Define ℓQ​(z):=12​‖μQ‖ℋ2−⟨μQ,φ⁡(z)⟩ℋ.\ell_{Q}(z):=\frac{1}{2}\|\mu_{Q}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}-\langle\mu_{Q},\varphi(z)\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}}. Its interventional risk Rπ​(Q):=∫𝒵ℓQ​(z)​Qπ​(𝑑z)R_{\pi}(Q):=\int_{{\mathcal{Z}}}\ell_{Q}(z)\,Q^{\pi}(dz) satisfies

Rπ​(Q)−Rπ​(Qπ)=ℱπ​(Q)=12​MMDk2⁡(Q,Qπ).R_{\pi}(Q)-R_{\pi}(Q^{\pi})=\mathcal{F}_{\pi}(Q)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{MMD}_{k}^{2}(Q,Q^{\pi}). (6)

Thus, excess interventional risk is exactly half the squared sampling discrepancy. Moreover, the part of the objective that determines optimization depends linearly on χ⁡(π)\chi(\pi). Recovering this one element therefore recovers the entire family of risks indexed by QQ.

3.2 Orthogonal representation of the interventional objective

Identification expresses χ⁡(π)\chi(\pi) under the observational law, but introduces unknown nuisance functions. Direct substitution of approximate nuisances can introduce first-order bias into the sampling objective. We instead seek an observed-data representation whose first-order nuisance sensitivity vanishes, as in orthogonal statistical learning [19].

Write 𝔼0\mathbb{E}_{0} for expectation under P0P_{0} and let PA,X​(d​a,d​x)=π0​(d​a∣x)​PX​(d​x)P_{A,X}(da,dx)=\pi_{0}(da\mid x)P_{X}(dx). The relevant nuisances are

m0​(a,x)\displaystyle m_{0}(a,x) :=𝔼0[φ(Z)∣A=a,X=x],w0(a,x):=dπ(⋅∣x)dπ0(⋅∣x)(a).\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\varphi(Z)\mid A=a,X=x],\quad w_{0}(a,x):=\frac{d\pi(\cdot\mid x)}{d\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x)}(a).

Proposition 2.2 yields two representations,

χ⁡(π)\displaystyle\chi(\pi) =𝔼0​[∫𝒜m0​(a,X)​π​(𝑑a∣X)]=𝔼0​[w0​(A,X)​φ​(Z)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0}\left[\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}m_{0}(a,X)\,\pi(da\mid X)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{0}[w_{0}(A,X)\varphi(Z)]. (7)

Either representation in Equation 7 could be used to construct the target embedding. A regression plug-in relies entirely on m0m_{0}, while inverse weighting relies entirely on w0w_{0}; errors in either representation therefore enter the resulting target at first order.

Instead, we combine the two through an augmented score, following the doubly robust RKHS construction [38, 62]. For candidate nuisance functions m:𝒜×𝒳→ℋm:{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathcal{H}} and w:𝒜×𝒳→ℝw:{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathbb{R}, write η=(m,w)\eta=(m,w) and define

Γη​(O)\displaystyle\Gamma_{\eta}(O) :=∫𝒜m⁡(a,X)​π​(𝑑a∣X)+w⁡(A,X)​{φ⁡(Z)−m⁡(A,X)},\displaystyle:=\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}m(a,X)\,\pi(da\mid X)+w(A,X)\{\varphi(Z)-m(A,X)\}, (8)

with population target hη:=𝔼0​[Γη​(O)]∈ℋ.h_{\eta}:=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\Gamma_{\eta}(O)]\in{\mathcal{H}}. The first term is the regression representation of the interventional embedding; the second uses the observed feature residual to correct it through intervention-to-observation reweighting.

Assumption 3.1 (Nuisance integrability).

Let PA,X​(d​a,d​x):=π0​(d​a∣x)​PX​(d​x)P_{A,X}(da,dx):=\pi_{0}(da\mid x)P_{X}(dx). The nuisance functions satisfy m,m0∈L2​(PA,X,ℋ)m,m_{0}\in L^{2}(P_{A,X};{\mathcal{H}}), and w,w0∈L2​(PA,X).w,w_{0}\in L^{2}(P_{A,X}).

Together with boundedness of kk, Assumption 3.1 ensures that Equation 8 is Bochner integrable and hηh_{\eta} is well defined. The L2L^{2} condition on w0w_{0} strengthens the absolute-continuity condition in Assumption 2.1 and controls the degree of intervention-to-observation reweighting.

Importantly, since the interventional MMD risk depends on the target only through χ⁡(π)\chi(\pi), the observed-data counterpart of the risk can be obtained simply by replacing χ⁡(π)\chi(\pi) with hηh_{\eta}:

R⁡(Q,η)\displaystyle R(Q;\eta) :=12​‖μQ‖ℋ2−⟨μQ,hη⟩ℋ=12​‖μQ−hη‖ℋ2−12​‖hη‖ℋ2.\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{2}\|\mu_{Q}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}-\langle\mu_{Q},h_{\eta}\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}}=\frac{1}{2}\|\mu_{Q}-h_{\eta}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|h_{\eta}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}. (9)

Thus, the same nuisance correction simultaneously defines the target for every candidate distribution QQ. This is the particular simplification of MMD that we exploit: unlike a generic nuisance-dependent generative risk, causal adjustment reduces to a single fixed Hilbert-space element.

Write rm:=‖m−m0‖L2​(PA,X,ℋ)r_{m}:=\|m-m_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P_{A,X};{\mathcal{H}})}, and rw:=‖w−w0‖L2​(PA,X)r_{w}:=\|w-w_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P_{A,X})}.

Proposition 3.2 (Double robustness and orthogonality).

Under Assumptions 2.1 and 3.1,

hη−χ⁡(π)\displaystyle h_{\eta}-\chi(\pi) =−𝔼0​[(w−w0)​(m−m0)],\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{0}\!\left[(w-w_{0})(m-m_{0})\right],
‖hη−χ⁡(π)‖ℋ\displaystyle\|h_{\eta}-\chi(\pi)\|_{{\mathcal{H}}} ≤rw​rm,\displaystyle\leq r_{w}r_{m}, (DR)

where the nuisance functions are evaluated at (A,X)(A,X). Hence hm,w0=hm0,w=χ⁡(π)h_{m,w_{0}}=h_{m_{0},w}=\chi(\pi), and therefore R⁡(Q,m,w0)=R⁡(Q,m0,w)=Rπ​(Q)R(Q;m,w_{0})=R(Q;m_{0},w)=R_{\pi}(Q) for every QQ.

Moreover, viewing R⁡(Q,η)R(Q;\eta) as a function of u=μQu=\mu_{Q}, its gradient with respect to uu is u−hηu-h_{\eta} and, for every square-integrable direction η˙\dot{\eta},

Dη​(u−hη)|η=η0​[η˙]=0,u∈ℋ,D_{\eta}\!\left(u-h_{\eta}\right)\big|_{\eta=\eta_{0}}[\dot{\eta}]=0,\qquad u\in{\mathcal{H}}, (ORTH)

where η0=(m0,w0)\eta_{0}=(m_{0},w_{0}).

The remainder in Equation DR is bilinear in the two nuisance errors, which yields both double robustness and first-order orthogonality. The proof is given in Appendix C.1.

Equation ORTH is the form of Neyman orthogonality relevant to the sampling problem: nuisance perturbations have no first-order effect on the gradient of the risk being optimized [10, 19]. In fact, the property holds for every candidate embedding uu, rather than only at the population minimizer. Therefore the nuisance-induced perturbation remains second order throughout the subsequent distributional optimization.

Remark 3.3.

This construction is related to doubly robust generative-risk correction [39], but MMD yields an additional simplification: because the target-dependent term is linear in the kernel mean embedding, orthogonalizing the entire family of sampling risks reduces to constructing the single target element hηh_{\eta}. The next subsection shows that the same element also determines the force driving the MMD transport.

3.3 Interventional MMD dynamics

We now turn the orthogonalized MMD objective into a transport sampler. Because the target enters only through a fixed RKHS element, we derive the dynamics for a generic h∈ℋh\in{\mathcal{H}}, covering both the exact target h=χ⁡(π)h=\chi(\pi) and its orthogonal representation h=hηh=h_{\eta}. We define

ℱh​(Q):=12​‖μQ−h‖ℋ2.\mathcal{F}_{h}(Q):=\frac{1}{2}\|\mu_{Q}-h\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}. (10)

When h=χ⁡(π)h=\chi(\pi), this is the interventional MMD objective in Equation 5. When h=hηh=h_{\eta}, it is the orthogonal population objective in Equation 9, up to a constant independent of QQ.

To turn Equation 10 into a spatial flow, we impose the following regularity conditions.

Assumption 3.4 (Flow regularity).

Let 𝒵=ℝdZ{\mathcal{Z}}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{Z}} and let Q0∈𝒫2​(𝒵)Q_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}({\mathcal{Z}}). The feature map φ:𝒵→ℋ\varphi:{\mathcal{Z}}\to{\mathcal{H}} is continuously Fréchet differentiable and, for finite constants Lφ,LDL_{\varphi},L_{D},

supz∈𝒵‖D​φ​(z)‖op\displaystyle\sup_{z\in{\mathcal{Z}}}\|D\varphi(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}} ≤Lφ,‖D​φ​(z)−D​φ​(z′)‖op≤LD​‖z−z′‖2.\displaystyle\leq L_{\varphi},\ \|D\varphi(z)-D\varphi(z^{\prime})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L_{D}\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}.

For the exact interventional flow, assume additionally Qπ∈𝒫2​(𝒵)Q^{\pi}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}({\mathcal{Z}}).

These conditions ensure that the velocity fields below are well defined and Lipschitz, so that the corresponding dynamics admit a well-defined measure-valued evolution in 𝒫2​(𝒵)\mathcal{P}_{2}({\mathcal{Z}}) [1, 2]. It can also be relaxed to local Lipschitzness [60].

For fixed hh, define the target potential sh​(z):=⟨h,φ⁡(z)⟩ℋs_{h}(z):=\langle h,\varphi(z)\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}} and the associated MMD witness fQ,h​(z):=⟨μQ−h,φ⁡(z)⟩ℋ=∫𝒵k⁡(z,z′)​Q​(d​z′)−sh​(z).f_{Q,h}(z):=\langle\mu_{Q}-h,\varphi(z)\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}}=\int_{{\mathcal{Z}}}k(z,z^{\prime})\,Q(dz^{\prime})-s_{h}(z). The first term depends on the current law QQ, whereas shs_{h} is a fixed target potential. Following MMD gradient flow [2], samples move along the negative spatial gradient of the witness,

vh​(Q,z)\displaystyle v_{h}(Q,z) :=−∇fQ,h(z)=−∫𝒵∇1k(z,z′)Q(dz′)+∇sh(z),\displaystyle:=-\nabla f_{Q,h}(z)=-\int_{{\mathcal{Z}}}\nabla_{1}k(z,z^{\prime})\,Q(dz^{\prime})+\nabla s_{h}(z),

where ∇1\nabla_{1} denotes differentiation in the first argument.

We define the Interventional MMD Flow (IMMD-F) as the law-valued evolution induced by vhv_{h}:

∂tQth+∇⋅(Qth​vh​(Qth,⋅))=0,Qt=0h=Q0.\partial_{t}Q_{t}^{h}+\nabla\cdot\bigl(Q_{t}^{h}v_{h}(Q_{t}^{h},\cdot)\bigr)=0,\ Q_{t=0}^{h}=Q_{0}. (IMMD-F)

Under Assumption 3.4, this evolution admits the characteristic representation

Z˙t=vh​(Qth,Zt),Z0∼Q0,\dot{Z}_{t}=v_{h}(Q_{t}^{h},Z_{t}),\qquad Z_{0}\sim Q_{0},

with Zt∼QthZ_{t}\sim Q_{t}^{h} for every t≥0t\geq 0. Hence the distributional optimization can be realized by transporting samples from Q0Q_{0}, which provides the basis for the interacting-particle procedure.

The generic target hh covers both constructions of interest: h=χ⁡(π)h=\chi(\pi) gives the ideal interventional flow, while h=hηh=h_{\eta} gives its orthogonal counterpart. By Proposition 3.2, the two coincide whenever either nuisance is correct.

We next characterize the descent of this flow and the effect of nuisance perturbations on its velocity field.

Proposition 3.5 (Dissipation and velocity stability).

Under Assumption 3.4, any sufficiently regular solution of equation IMMD-F satisfies

dd​tℱh(Qth)=−∫𝒵∥vh(Qth,z)∥22Qth(dz)≤0.\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{F}_{h}(Q_{t}^{h})=-\int_{{\mathcal{Z}}}\|v_{h}(Q_{t}^{h},z)\|_{2}^{2}\,Q_{t}^{h}(dz)\leq 0. (11)

Moreover, for every Q∈𝒫2​(𝒵)Q\in\mathcal{P}_{2}({\mathcal{Z}}),

supz∈𝒵‖vhη​(Q,z)−vχ⁡(π)​(Q,z)‖2\displaystyle\sup_{z\in{\mathcal{Z}}}\|v_{h_{\eta}}(Q,z)-v_{\chi(\pi)}(Q,z)\|_{2} ≤Lφ​‖hη−χ⁡(π)‖ℋ≤Lφ​rw​rm.\displaystyle\leq L_{\varphi}\|h_{\eta}-\chi(\pi)\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}\leq L_{\varphi}r_{w}r_{m}. (VEL)

Equation 11 shows that IMMD Flow decreases the objective associated with its target hh. As for standard MMD gradient flow, this dissipation alone does not guarantee convergence to the global minimizer [2].

Equation VEL gives the dynamical consequence of orthogonality: nuisance error perturbs the transport velocity only at product order. Controlling how this perturbation propagates to trajectories and the generated distribution is deferred to the convergence analysis.

4 Sampling Procedure

We estimate the interventional target from observational data, then hold it fixed while evolving particles. Note that no nuisance refitting or additional sampling network is required during generation.

4.1 Orthogonal target estimation

Given O1,…,On​∼iid​P0O_{1},\ldots,O_{n}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}P_{0}, set Zi=E⁡(Yi)Z_{i}=E(Y_{i}) and fit η^=(m^,w^)\widehat{\eta}=(\widehat{m},\widehat{w}). We estimate the target by averaging the orthogonal score in equation 8:

h^π:=1n​∑i=1nΓη^​(Oi).\widehat{h}_{\pi}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma_{\widehat{\eta}}(O_{i}). (12)

Our implementation fits and evaluates the nuisances on the same observations; its statistical conditions are stated in the convergence analysis.

Projected Nyström construction. To reduce regression cost, we fit m^\widehat{m} in an input-side Nyström subspace [53], using kernels kX,kAk_{X},k_{A}, mLm_{L} uniformly sampled landmarks, and ridge parameter λ>0\lambda>0. Intervention integrals are approximated with JJ independent draws from π(⋅∣Xi)\pi(\cdot\mid X_{i}) per context. The resulting numerical target and its potential are

h~π\displaystyle\widetilde{h}_{\pi} =∑i=1nvDR,i​φ​(Zi),s~π​(z)=∑i=1nvDR,i​k​(z,Zi).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{\mathrm{DR},i}\varphi(Z_{i}),\kern 5.0pt\widetilde{s}_{\pi}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{\mathrm{DR},i}k(z,Z_{i}). (13)

Here h^π\widehat{h}_{\pi} uses the projected regression with exact intervention integrals, whereas h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} denotes its numerical realization. Appendix B.2 gives the coefficient construction; the full-kernel alternative is in Appendix B.1. The coefficients may be signed and need not sum to one, so zero residual against h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} is not assumed.

4.2 Particle generation

We instantiate IMMD Flow with h=h~πh=\widetilde{h}_{\pi}. Draw Yj(0)​∼iid​PinitY_{j}^{(0)}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}P_{\rm init} and set Zj(0)=E⁡(Yj(0))Z_{j}^{(0)}=E(Y_{j}^{(0)}), choosing PinitP_{\rm init} so that Q0=E#​Pinit∈𝒫2​(𝒵)Q_{0}=E_{\#}P_{\rm init}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}({\mathcal{Z}}). At iteration rr, the current law is approximated by Q^M(r)=M−1​∑j=1MδZj(r)\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)}=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta_{Z_{j}^{(r)}}. Following Arbel et al. [2] and Chen et al. [9], we optionally perturb the gradient evaluation locations: set Z~j(r)=Zj(r)+βr​Uj(r)\widetilde{Z}_{j}^{(r)}=Z_{j}^{(r)}+\beta_{r}U_{j}^{(r)}, with fresh, independent Uj(r)∼𝒩⁡(0,IdZ)U_{j}^{(r)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d_{Z}}) and βr=cβ​(r+1)−α\beta_{r}=c_{\beta}(r+1)^{-\alpha}, where cβ≥0c_{\beta}\geq 0 and α∈[0,1/2)\alpha\in[0,1/2). For step sizes ηr>0\eta_{r}>0, update

Gj(r)\displaystyle G_{j}^{(r)} =1M​∑ℓ=1M∇1k​(Z~j(r),Zℓ(r))−∇s~π​(Z~j(r)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\nabla_{1}k(\widetilde{Z}_{j}^{(r)},Z_{\ell}^{(r)})-\nabla\widetilde{s}_{\pi}(\widetilde{Z}_{j}^{(r)}), (14)
Zj(r+1)\displaystyle Z_{j}^{(r+1)} =Zj(r)−ηr​Gj(r).\displaystyle=Z_{j}^{(r)}-\eta_{r}G_{j}^{(r)}.

All gradients use the same current particle cloud; only their evaluation locations are perturbed. Setting cβ=0c_{\beta}=0 recovers the Euler particle update. The target coefficients remain fixed.

After RR updates, decode once with a fixed D:𝒵→𝒴D:{\mathcal{Z}}\to{\mathcal{Y}} and return Q^M(R)\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(R)} and P^M=D#​Q^M(R)\widehat{P}_{M}=D_{\#}\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(R)}. Taking E=D=IdE=D=\mathrm{Id} recovers outcome-space sampling. The generated particles need not be independent. Algorithm 1 specifies the smooth-kernel sampler; the Riesz–AdamW variant uses a distinct energy and update rule (see Appendix E.2).

5 Statistical Guarantees

In this section, we bound the discrepancy between the generated empirical distribution and QπQ^{\pi}, accounting for the error in the target used by the sampler. Recall that h^π\widehat{h}_{\pi} in Equation 12 is the doubly robust target estimator with intervention integrals evaluated exactly, whereas h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} in Equation 13 is its numerical approximation. Write

en,J:=‖h~π−χ⁡(π)‖ℋ.e_{n,J}:=\|\widetilde{h}_{\pi}-\chi(\pi)\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}.

We first control sampling error in terms of en,Je_{n,J} in Section 5.1, then bound this quantity using orthogonal target estimation in Section 5.2. The representation, decoder, and kernels are fixed independently of the observations analyzed here.

5.1 IMMD-Flow sampling error

A growing body of work studies the MMD-flow error, establishing conditions under which it vanishes as the number of particles MM and iterations RR increase. Existing approaches include entropy regularization [59], noise injection [2, 9], adaptive kernel lengthscales [29], Fisher–Rao geometry [5, 4], and energy/Riesz kernels [16, 11, 12, 51]. For finite-particle analysis, we consider the noise-injection framework of Arbel et al. [2], Chen et al. [9], because it gives explicit finite-iteration and finite-particle bounds for smooth kernels.

Assumption 5.1 (Smooth particle dynamics).

The feature map φ\varphi is twice continuously Fréchet differentiable. Its norm and the operator norms of its first two derivatives are uniformly bounded by κ≥1\kappa\geq 1. The update uses a constant step size ηr≡τ>0\eta_{r}\equiv\tau>0 and noise levels βr=cβ​(r+1)−α\beta_{r}=c_{\beta}(r+1)^{-\alpha}, where

12​τ​κ2​dZ≤1,0<cβ≤12​dZ,0≤α<12.12\tau\kappa^{2}d_{Z}\leq 1,\qquad 0<c_{\beta}\leq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{d_{Z}}},\qquad 0\leq\alpha<\frac{1}{2}.

Smoothness alone does not ensure convergence to the target. As in noise-injected MMD-flow analysis [2, 9], we additionally impose a gradient-dominance condition over the iterations being analyzed. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} contain all observations and target-construction randomness, and let ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r} additionally contain the initial particles and the Gaussian perturbations before iteration rr.

Assumption 5.2 (Noisy gradient dominance).

For r=0,…,R−1r=0,\ldots,R-1, the particles generated with target h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} satisfy, almost surely,

1M​∑j=1M𝔼⁡[‖vχ⁡(π)​(Q^M(r),Zj(r)+βr​Uj(r))‖22|ℱr]≥4​κ2​dZ​βr2​MMDk2⁡(Q^M(r),Qπ),\displaystyle\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|v_{\chi(\pi)}\bigl(\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)},Z_{j}^{(r)}+\beta_{r}U_{j}^{(r)}\bigr)\right\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{r}\right]\geq 4\kappa^{2}d_{Z}\beta_{r}^{2}\operatorname{MMD}_{k}^{2}(\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)},Q^{\pi}), (15)

where Uj(r)U_{j}^{(r)} are independent standard Gaussian vectors.

This condition evaluates the true-target velocity along the estimated-target particle process. It is an additional optimization assumption, rather than a consequence of the prescribed noise schedule or nuisance orthogonality. We impose this condition to establish a favorable convergence rate, rather than because it is necessary for the good performance of MMD flows. Indeed, as shown by Logarajah et al. [36], a sufficiently large number of interacting particles can also guarantee good performance without a prescribed noise schedule.

Theorem 5.3 (Estimated-target particle bound).

Under Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2, there exist constants C0,C1,C2>0C_{0},C_{1},C_{2}>0 depending only on κ,dZ,τ,cβ,α\kappa,d_{Z},\tau,c_{\beta},\alpha such that, for R≥1R\geq 1 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1),

MMDk⁡(Q^M(R),Qπ)≤C0​exp⁡(−τ​κ2​dZ​cβ216​(1−2​α)​R1−2​α)+(1+C1​Rα)​en,J+C2​Rα​log⁡(R/δ)M.\displaystyle\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(R)},Q^{\pi})\leq C_{0}\exp\left(-\frac{\tau\kappa^{2}d_{Z}c_{\beta}^{2}}{16(1-2\alpha)}R^{1-2\alpha}\right)+(1+C_{1}R^{\alpha})e_{n,J}+C_{2}R^{\alpha}\sqrt{\frac{\log(R/\delta)}{M}}. (16)

For each realization of 𝒟\mathcal{D} satisfying ‖h~π‖ℋ≤κ\|\widetilde{h}_{\pi}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}\leq\kappa, this bound holds with conditional probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over particle initialization and update noise.

Proof is given in Appendix D.2. The three terms describe optimization decay, propagated numerical target error, and finite-particle error. Increasing the iteration number RR reduces the first optimization error term, but amplifies the second target numerical error. The boundedness condition that ‖h~π‖ℋ≤κ\|\tilde{h}_{\pi}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\kappa holds with probability tending to one under the assumptions of the next Corollary 5.6, as established in Equation 121.

5.2 Statistical and numerical target error

To apply Theorem 5.3, we control the numerical target relative to χ⁡(π)\chi(\pi). Let η^n=(m^n,w^n)\widehat{\eta}_{n}=(\widehat{m}_{n},\widehat{w}_{n}) denote the fitted nuisances, and write Pn​g=n−1​∑ig⁡(Oi)P_{n}g=n^{-1}\sum_{i}g(O_{i}) and P0​g=𝔼0​[g⁡(O)]P_{0}g=\mathbb{E}_{0}[g(O)].

Assumption 5.4 (Nuisance estimation and sample reuse).

For deterministic rates rm,n,rw,nr_{m,n},r_{w,n},

‖m^n−m0‖L2​(PA,X,ℋ)\displaystyle\|\widehat{m}_{n}-m_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P_{A,X};{\mathcal{H}})} =Op​(rm,n),‖w^n−w0‖L2​(PA,X)=Op​(rw,n).\displaystyle=O_{p}(r_{m,n}),\quad\|\widehat{w}_{n}-w_{0}\|_{L^{2}(P_{A,X})}=O_{p}(r_{w,n}).

The oracle score has finite second moment, and

‖(Pn−P0){Γη^n−Γη0}‖ℋ=Op(n−1/2),\left\|(P_{n}-P_{0})\{\Gamma_{\widehat{\eta}_{n}}-\Gamma_{\eta_{0}}\}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}=O_{p}(n^{-1/2}), (17)

where η0=(m0,w0)\eta_{0}=(m_{0},w_{0}).

Condition equation 17 accounts for fitting and evaluating the nuisances on the same observations; a regression prediction rate alone does not establish it. For intervention integration, define m¯n​(Xi):=∫m^n​(a,Xi)​π​(𝑑a∣Xi)\bar{m}_{n}(X_{i}):=\int\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})\,\pi(da\mid X_{i}) and

Vn:=1n​∑i=1n∫‖m^n​(a,Xi)−m¯n​(Xi)‖ℋ2​π​(𝑑a∣Xi).V_{n}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int\|\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})-\bar{m}_{n}(X_{i})\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}^{2}\,\pi(da\mid X_{i}).
Proposition 5.5 (Accuracy of the numerical target).

Under Assumptions 2.1, 3.1, and 5.4, suppose that, conditional on the observations, landmarks, and fitted nuisances, intervention integration uses JJ independent draws per context, also independent across contexts, and that Vn=Op​(1)V_{n}=O_{p}(1). For exact projected regression and its finite-JJ target,

en,J=Op(n−1/2+rm,nrw,n+(nJ)−1/2).e_{n,J}=O_{p}\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{m,n}r_{w,n}+(nJ)^{-1/2}\right).

The product term follows from equation DR; the Monte Carlo term follows from the conditional mean-square error Vn/(n​J)V_{n}/(nJ) in Lemma D.22. Thus a fixed J≥1J\geq 1 preserves the statistical rate when VnV_{n} is tight. Under the projected Nyström conditions of Theorem D.16, substituting rm,n=n−1/[2(1+γ)]r_{m,n}=n^{-1/[2(1+\gamma)]} gives

en,J=Op(n−1/2+rw,nn−12​(1+γ)+(nJ)−1/2),e_{n,J}=O_{p}\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{w,n}n^{-\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma)}}+(nJ)^{-1/2}\right), (18)

where γ\gamma is the input-capacity exponent; see Assumption D.5. This specialization requires the stated ridge and growing-landmark conditions.

5.3 Consistency

Now, we are ready to combine Theorem 5.3 and Proposition 5.5 to obtain the final consistency result. To give an explicit choice of computational budgets RR and particle number MM as a function of the target sample size nn, suppose that the nuisance-error product satisfies rm,n​rw,n=O⁡(n−s)r_{m,n}r_{w,n}=O(n^{-s}) for some s∈(0,1/2]s\in(0,1/2].

Corollary 5.6.

Suppose the assumptions of Theorem 5.3 and Proposition 5.5 hold over the chosen iteration horizons, with constants independent of nn. We further take κ>supz∈𝒵‖φ⁡(z)‖ℋ\kappa>\sup_{z\in{\mathcal{Z}}}\|\varphi(z)\|_{\mathcal{H}}. Assume that rm,n​rw,n=O⁡(n−s)r_{m,n}r_{w,n}=O(n^{-s}) for some s∈(0,1/2]s\in(0,1/2], and fix J≥1J\geq 1. Let CR=16​s​(1−2​α)τ​κ2​dZ​cβ2C_{R}=\frac{16s(1-2\alpha)}{\tau\kappa^{2}d_{Z}c_{\beta}^{2}}. Choose the iteration and particle budgets as

Rn=⌈(CR​log⁡n)1/(1−2​α)⌉,Mn=⌈n2​s​log⁡log⁡n⌉,R_{n}=\left\lceil({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}C_{R}}\log n)^{1/(1-2\alpha)}\right\rceil,\quad M_{n}=\left\lceil n^{2s}\log\log n\right\rceil, (19)

Then, MMDk⁡(Q^Mn(Rn),Qπ)=Op​(n−s​(log⁡n)α/(1−2​α)).\operatorname{MMD}_{k}\bigl(\widehat{Q}_{M_{n}}^{(R_{n})},Q^{\pi}\bigr)=O_{p}\!\left(n^{-s}(\log n)^{\alpha/(1-2\alpha)}\right).

If MMDk\operatorname{MMD}_{k} metrizes weak convergence [55], the generated empirical distribution also converges weakly to the interventional distribution QπQ^{\pi}.

Finally, for encoded outcomes, the remaining step is to transfer latent accuracy through the decoder.

Proposition 5.7 (Outcome-space transfer).

Let kE​(y,y′):=k⁡(E⁡(y),E⁡(y′))k_{E}(y,y^{\prime}):=k(E(y),E(y^{\prime})). If E,DE,D are measurable and φ\varphi is LkL_{k}-Lipschitz, then, MMDkE⁡(D#​Q,Pπ)≤MMDk⁡(Q,Qπ)+Lk​𝔼Z∼Q​‖E⁡(D⁡(Z))−Z‖2.\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{E}}(D_{\#}Q,P^{\pi})\leq\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(Q,Q^{\pi})+L_{k}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q}\|E(D(Z))-Z\|_{2}.

Applying this bound to Q=Q^M(R)Q=\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(R)} adds only the displayed cycle-reconstruction error to the latent guarantee. When EE is non-injective, convergence in kEk_{E} need not identify the full outcome law. If DD is continuous and D#​Qπ=PπD_{\#}Q^{\pi}=P^{\pi}, latent weak consistency also yields weak consistency of the decoded outcomes. Taking E=D=IdE=D=\mathrm{Id} removes this transfer step.

6 Numerical Experiments

Methods. We evaluate our orthogonal variant of our IMMD-Flow method, that we write DR–IMMD (for the Doubly Robust embedding) together with two variants of MMD flow using plug-in estimates of the interventional embedding. Plug-in–IMMD constructs the fixed target using only the fitted conditional mean embedding, whereas IPW–IMMD uses only the estimated intervention-to-logging density ratio. DR–IMMD combines both through the orthogonal score in Section 3. These variants differ only in the target coefficients supplied to the flow. Their exact constructions are given in Appendix B.

We compare against Deconfounding Flow Matching (DecFM) [15], which is formulated for arm-specific counterfactual distributions corresponding to hard interventions A←aA\leftarrow a. Since hard interventions are a special case of our framework, with π(⋅∣x)=δa\pi(\cdot\mid x)=\delta_{a}, we specialize IMMD-Flow accordingly for ColorMNIST and CelebA. For structured outcomes, we run DecFM in the same fixed latent representation, encoding with EE and decoding with DD, and report its plug-in, DR-I, and DR-OT variants. We do not report DecFM on dSprites, whose target is a context-dependent soft intervention π(⋅∣X)\pi(\cdot\mid X).

Benchmarks. We evaluate the methods on three image-valued deconfounding tasks. ColorMNIST, adapted from Dance et al. [15], couples treatment-specific digit identity with a context variable that affects both treatment assignment and foreground colour. The interventional target fixes the digit class while averaging over the population distribution of the colour-generating context, thereby removing the observational colour imbalance.

The CelebA benchmark of Dance et al. [15] sets A=SexA=\mathrm{Sex} and X=HairColorX=\mathrm{HairColor}, with the observational data constructed so that hair color has different distributions across the two sex groups. For each target value aa, the interventional law replaces the group-specific context distribution PX|A=aP_{X\mid A=a} underlying PY|A=aP_{Y\mid A=a} by the population distribution PXP_{X}. The task is therefore to generate images with attribute A=aA=a while correcting the observational hair-colour imbalance. Finally, we consider the continuous actions setting Zenati et al. [62] over soft interventions. The context determines sprite shape and scale and also affects a stochastic action controlling position. The target policy changes the conditional action distribution and hence the joint distribution of visual content and position. Full descriptions of the data-generating processes are given in Appendix E.3.

Results. We evaluate generated samples using empirical sliced 22-Wasserstein distance in decoded pixel space (SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2}) and encoder latent space (Lat. SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2}) [8], together with FID on decoded images [26]; lower is better. All experiments in this section use n=20,000n=20{,}000, M=2,000M=2{,}000, and three data seeds, with results for static interventions averaged over the two arms within each seed.

Sample quality. Table 1 shows that all IMMD variants outperform every DecFM baseline in pixel-space SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} on ColorMNIST and CelebA. DR–IMMD also achieves the best latent SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} on CelebA, lower FID than all DecFM variants on ColorMNIST, and comparable FID to the best DecFM result on CelebA. Across all three benchmarks, DR–IMMD performs competitively with the better single-nuisance variant, without the benchmark-specific degradations observed for Plug-in–IMMD on CelebA and IPW–IMMD on ColorMNIST.

Computational efficiency. A central advantage of IMMD-Flow is that it avoids training an intervention-specific generative model. Once the nuisance functions have been estimated, the target kernel embedding is constructed directly and held fixed, and samples are generated by evolving a finite collection of particles under the resulting MMD flow. In contrast, DecFM learns a neural velocity field through flow matching for the interventional distribution.

Table 2 compares one-time fitting and post-fitting sample generation on ColorMNIST and CelebA. For DR–IMMD, fitting comprises learning the nuisance functions—the conditional mean embedding and intervention-to-logging density ratio—and constructing the fixed orthogonal RKHS target. During sampling, these quantities remain fixed while M=2,000M=2{,}000 particles are iteratively transported under the resulting MMD flow. For DecFM, fitting instead consists of training the neural velocity field through flow matching, while sampling transports particles by integrating the learned flow. Shared representation preprocessing, decoding, and metric evaluation are excluded from all reported timings. At n=20,000n=20{,}000 and M=2,000M=2{,}000, DR–IMMD reduces total fitting-and-generation time by 11.011.0–42.2×42.2\times on ColorMNIST and 12.612.6–41.3×41.3\times on CelebA relative to the DecFM variants. This advantage is driven by the fitting stage: DR–IMMD constructs its fixed Hilbert-space target in seconds, whereas DecFM must train a neural flow-matching model. Conversely, once fitting is complete, DecFM generates samples faster than the iterative IMMD particle optimizer. The comparison therefore demonstrates a substantial end-to-end computational advantage at the reported sampling scale, rather than an advantage in post-fitting sampling time.

Particle evolution. Following Dance et al. [15], we initialize particles from the observational distribution PY|A=aP_{Y\mid A=a}, which already contains much of the image structure present in the interventional target. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting deconfounding process on ColorMNIST. As the particles evolve, their foreground colours change while their digit identities are largely preserved. At the population level, the colour distribution moves from the confounded observational law towards the oracle interventional distribution PXP_{X}. Thus, the flow primarily corrects the observational colour imbalance while preserving the remaining image structure.

Figure 2 illustrates a similar process on CelebA, where particles undergo gradual changes in appearance, including hair colour, while much of their original facial structure remains recognisable. In both cases, these changes arise from optimizing the particle locations against a fixed estimate of the interventional kernel embedding, with the decoder held fixed throughout. The resulting trajectories illustrate how initializing from observational samples allows the flow to exploit their existing structure when approximating the interventional distribution.

Ablations. Appendices E.5 and E.6 provide additional qualitative samples, particle trajectories, and ablations over sample size, particle count, initialization, confounding, and Nyström approximation. Sampling generally improves with more logged data and consistently with more particles. Observational initialization is particularly beneficial on the harder image benchmarks, while performance degrades only gradually as overlap weakens.

7 Conclusion

We introduced IMMD-Flow, which turns an estimated interventional RKHS target into samples through particle transport, without training an additional sampler. The framework accommodates both supported hard interventions and context-dependent stochastic policies, including continuous-action policies. Its doubly robust, orthogonal target yields product-order perturbations of the transport dynamics. Projected Nyström enables reuse across interventions. On ColorMNIST and CelebA, IMMD-Flow improves pixel-space SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} over the DecFM baselines and reduces total fitting-and-sampling time by 1111–42×42\times at the reported sampling scale, while achieving comparable FID. A limitation is reliance on standard observed-confounding and overlap assumptions.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Discussion of Related work

Debiased estimation of interventional distributions.

A growing literature extends semiparametric debiasing methods from scalar causal estimands to entire interventional or counterfactual outcome distributions. Early work developed efficient estimators for projections and functionals of counterfactual densities, including truncated-series and exponential-family approximations [30]. More recent methods combine these ideas with flexible generative models. Interventional Normalizing Flows Melnychuk et al. [43] parameterize the target interventional density by a normalizing flow and optimize a one-step corrected likelihood objective, while Martinez-Taboada and Kennedy [40] use a doubly robust Kernel Stein Discrepancy to estimate an energy-based counterfactual density. Luedtke and Fukumizu [39] give a more general doubly robust construction for generative training objectives, with instantiations including diffusion models and flow matching. Dance et al. [15] learn a flow from the observational treatment-conditional distribution to the interventional distribution, thereby exploiting geometric structure shared by the observed and target laws rather than generating the latter from a fixed generic base distribution. A common limitation of these approaches is that sampling from each interventional distribution of interest requires fitting a corresponding generative model, in addition to estimating the causal nuisances. This can be especially costly in high-dimensional settings, when multiple interventional distributions are of interest. IMMD-Flow instead avoids target-model training by formulating sampling as distributional optimization. For MMD, the target distribution is represented by a single kernel mean embedding, which admits a closed-form orthogonal estimator from observational data. Sampling then reduces to directly optimizing a particle approximation toward this estimated embedding.

Kernel embeddings of interventional distributions.

Our target representation builds directly on work representing causal outcome distributions by kernel mean embeddings. Muandet et al. [45] introduced counterfactual mean embeddings (CMEs), which identify interventional outcome distributions nonparametrically in an RKHS and permit distributional comparison as well as sample reconstruction by kernel herding. Subsequent work developed doubly robust versions of these embeddings for distributional treatment-effect testing [18], while Luedtke and Chung [38] developed general one-step theory for Hilbert-valued causal parameters, including counterfactual kernel mean embeddings. More recently, Zenati et al. [62] introduced counterfactual policy mean embeddings for distributional treatment effects under soft interventions, deriving doubly robust estimators for general target policies together with tests (see also [63]) and a kernel-herding procedure for generating representative counterfactual samples [55]. Our method uses the same doubly robust kernel embedding, but as a fixed target for distributional optimization. Instead of kernel herding, IMMD-Flow jointly transports particles under the MMD gradient flow, allowing initialization from a useful source distribution such as ℙY|A=a\mathbb{P}_{Y\mid A=a}, while propagating embedding-estimation error directly through the sampling dynamics.

MMD-based particle transport.

Methodologically, our sampling stage is related to nonparametric generative methods based on kernel discrepancies and Wasserstein gradient flows. MMD provides a metric on probability measures for characteristic kernels [21, 58], and Arbel et al. [2] introduced the Wasserstein gradient flow of MMD together with interacting-particle approximations and noise regularization. Subsequent work has studied alternative kernels, regularization schemes, and scalable or deep versions of MMD transport [25, 20, 9]. Recent analyses have further clarified convergence properties of MMD and energy-kernel gradient flows. These methods assume that the target distribution, or samples from it, are available. Our setting introduces an additional causal-estimation layer: samples from the target interventional law are unobserved, and the force driving the particle dynamics is instead constructed from an estimated interventional mean embedding. The main connection between the two parts of our method is therefore that causal estimation error appears as a perturbation of the target potential in the MMD flow. This permits us to combine orthogonal estimation of the interventional distribution with particle-level transport guarantees in a single error analysis.

Counterfactual sampling.

Our work is also related to the broader literature on sampling from counterfactual distributions, including structural causal models and counterfactual transport methods [47, 54, 27, 14]. A key distinction is that IMMD-Flow targets the marginal interventional law ℙπ\mathbb{P}^{\pi}, rather than unit-level counterfactual distributions such as ℙπ(⋅∣Y=y)\mathbb{P}^{\pi}(\cdot\mid Y=y). Consequently, although particles may be initialized from ℙY|A=a\mathbb{P}_{Y\mid A=a} and transported to ℙπ\mathbb{P}^{\pi}, the resulting particle trajectories do not define unit-level counterfactual couplings. Such an interpretation requires additional cross-world or structural assumptions beyond those needed to identify ℙπ\mathbb{P}^{\pi}.

Appendix B Orthogonal Target Computation

This appendix derives the orthogonal Hilbert-space target used by IMMD-Flow. We first give the full kernel-ridge computation, then derive its input-projected Nyström approximation. We subsequently describe the Monte Carlo approximation of the intervention integrals and compare the computational costs of the two constructions. Throughout, the target-policy integral is treated separately from its finite-JJ approximation.

B.1 Full-ridge computation

Let K∈ℝn×nK\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be the corresponding Gram matrix, Ki​j=kS​(Si,Sj)K_{ij}=k_{S}(S_{i},S_{j}), and define

For s=(a,x)s=(a,x), let

ks=(kS​(S1,s),…,kS​(Sn,s))⊤.k_{s}=\bigl(k_{S}(S_{1},s),\ldots,k_{S}(S_{n},s)\bigr)^{\top}.

The vector-valued kernel-ridge estimator of the conditional mean embedding is

m^full​(s)=∑j=1n[Bλ​ks]j​φ​(Zj).\widehat{m}_{\rm full}(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}[B_{\lambda}k_{s}]_{j}\,\varphi(Z_{j}). (20)

and collect these vectors as

Kπ:=(k¯π,1,…,k¯π,n)∈ℝn×n.K_{\pi}:=\bigl(\bar{k}_{\pi,1},\ldots,\bar{k}_{\pi,n}\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.

For the product kernel above, this matrix can equivalently be written as

Kπ=KX⊙KA,π,K_{\pi}=K_{X}\odot K_{A,\pi},

where

[KA,π]j​i:=∫𝒜kA​(Aj,a)​π​(𝑑a∣Xi).[K_{A,\pi}]_{ji}:=\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}k_{A}(A_{j},a)\,\pi(da\mid X_{i}). (22)

Writing

𝒘^=(w^​(A1,X1),…,w^​(An,Xn))⊤,\widehat{\bm{w}}=\bigl(\widehat{w}(A_{1},X_{1}),\ldots,\widehat{w}(A_{n},X_{n})\bigr)^{\top},

bfull\displaystyle b^{\rm full} =Bλ​(Kπ​𝟏n−K​𝒘^),vfull=1n​(bfull+𝒘^).\displaystyle=B_{\lambda}\left(K_{\pi}\mathbf{1}_{n}-K\widehat{\bm{w}}\right),\kern 5.0ptv_{\rm full}=\frac{1}{n}\left(b^{\rm full}+\widehat{\bm{w}}\right). (24)

vfull=vPI,full+1n​(𝒘^−Bλ​K​𝒘^).v_{\rm full}=v_{\mathrm{PI,full}}+\frac{1}{n}\left(\widehat{\bm{w}}-B_{\lambda}K\widehat{\bm{w}}\right). (26)

Thus, once the regression system is solved, changing the intervention affects the estimator only through the intervention integrals and, when target-specific, the density-ratio nuisance.

B.2 Projected Nyström computation

The full construction requires solving an n×nn\times n kernel system. We instead restrict the conditional mean embedding regression to a Nyström subspace of the input RKHS [53, 17].

Select landmark indices

L={ℓ1,…,ℓmL}⊆{1,…,n}L=\{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m_{L}}\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}

uniformly without replacement, and write

S~q:=Sℓq.\widetilde{S}_{q}:=S_{\ell_{q}}.

Define

Ci​q\displaystyle C_{iq} :=kS​(Si,S~q),\displaystyle:=k_{S}(S_{i},\widetilde{S}_{q}), Wq​r\displaystyle W_{qr} :=kS​(S~q,S~r),\displaystyle:=k_{S}(\widetilde{S}_{q},\widetilde{S}_{r}), (27)

so that

C∈ℝn×mL,W∈ℝmL×mL.C\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m_{L}},\qquad W\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{L}\times m_{L}}.

Let

Gλ:=(C⊤​C+n​λ​W)†,G_{\lambda}:=\left(C^{\top}C+n\lambda W\right)^{\dagger}, (28)

where †\dagger denotes the Moore–Penrose inverse when required.

For s=(a,x)s=(a,x), define the landmark kernel vector

cs=(kS​(S~1,s),…,kS​(S~mL,s))⊤.c_{s}=\bigl(k_{S}(\widetilde{S}_{1},s),\ldots,k_{S}(\widetilde{S}_{m_{L}},s)\bigr)^{\top}.

The projected estimator can then be written directly in the logged-outcome basis as

m^Nys​(s)=∑i=1n[C​Gλ​cs]i​φ​(Zi).\widehat{m}_{\rm Nys}(s)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[CG_{\lambda}c_{s}]_{i}\,\varphi(Z_{i}). (29)

For each context XiX_{i}, define

c¯π,i:=∫𝒜c(a,Xi)​π​(𝑑a∣Xi)∈ℝmL,\bar{c}_{\pi,i}:=\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}c_{(a,X_{i})}\,\pi(da\mid X_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{L}}, (30)

and let

Cπ:=(c¯π,1,…,c¯π,n)∈ℝmL×n.C_{\pi}:=\bigl(\bar{c}_{\pi,1},\ldots,\bar{c}_{\pi,n}\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{L}\times n}.

Because the landmarks are selected from the logged inputs,

Cπ=(Kπ)L:.C_{\pi}=(K_{\pi})_{L:}.

Thus the projected construction evaluates the exact intervention-integrated regression contrast only at the landmarks.

Substituting equation 29 into the orthogonal score gives

bproj\displaystyle b^{\rm proj} =C​Gλ​(Cπ​𝟏n−C⊤​𝒘^),vDR=1n​(bproj+𝒘^).\displaystyle=CG_{\lambda}\left(C_{\pi}\mathbf{1}_{n}-C^{\top}\widehat{\bm{w}}\right),\kern 5.0ptv_{\rm DR}=\frac{1}{n}\left(b^{\rm proj}+\widehat{\bm{w}}\right). (31)

h^π,Nys=∑i=1nvDR,i​φ​(Zi).\widehat{h}_{\pi,\rm Nys}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{{\rm DR},i}\varphi(Z_{i}). (32)

The projection acts on the input-side regression problem only: equation 32 still expands over all nn logged outcome features. This distinction is relevant to the particle-stage complexity.

Whitened landmark coordinates.

For numerical stability, let

W=Vr​Dr​Vr⊤W=V_{r}D_{r}V_{r}^{\top}

denote the eigendecomposition of WW on its retained positive eigenspace, and define

RW:=VrDr−1/2,Φ:=CRW.R_{W}:=V_{r}D_{r}^{-1/2},\qquad\Phi:=CR_{W}.

Writing

rπ:=Cπ​𝟏n−C⊤​𝒘^,qπ:=RW⊤​rπ,r_{\pi}:=C_{\pi}\mathbf{1}_{n}-C^{\top}\widehat{\bm{w}},\qquad q_{\pi}:=R_{W}^{\top}r_{\pi}, (33)

bproj=Φ​(Φ⊤​Φ+n​λ​Ir)−1​qπ.b^{\rm proj}=\Phi\left(\Phi^{\top}\Phi+n\lambda I_{r}\right)^{-1}q_{\pi}. (34)

Using all positive eigenpairs is only a change of coordinates within the landmark subspace. Discarding additional positive eigenvalues through a numerical threshold introduces a further subspace approximation.

C~π(J)=(K~π(J))L:.\widetilde{C}_{\pi}^{(J)}=\bigl(\widetilde{K}_{\pi}^{(J)}\bigr)_{L:}.

Replacing CπC_{\pi} by C~π(J)\widetilde{C}_{\pi}^{(J)} in equation 31 gives

b~Jproj\displaystyle\widetilde{b}_{J}^{\rm proj} :=C​Gλ​(C~π(J)​𝟏n−C⊤​𝒘^),v~DR,J:=1n​(b~Jproj+𝒘^).\displaystyle:=CG_{\lambda}\left(\widetilde{C}_{\pi}^{(J)}\mathbf{1}_{n}-C^{\top}\widehat{\bm{w}}\right),\kern 5.0pt\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{DR},J}:=\frac{1}{n}\left(\widetilde{b}_{J}^{\rm proj}+\widehat{\bm{w}}\right). (39)

The resulting numerical target is

h~π,Nys,J:=∑i=1nv~DR,J,i​φ​(Zi).\widetilde{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{Nys},J}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{DR},J,i}\varphi(Z_{i}). (40)

This is the finite-JJ target denoted by h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} in the main text:

h~π=h~π,Nys,J.\widetilde{h}_{\pi}=\widetilde{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{Nys},J}.

Similarly, h^π=h^π,Nys\widehat{h}_{\pi}=\widehat{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{Nys}} denotes the projected estimator with exact intervention integration.

Let ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} contain the logged sample, selected landmarks, and fitted nuisance estimates, prior to drawing the target-policy actions. Conditional on ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n},

𝔼⁡[K~π(J)∣ℱn]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{K}_{\pi}^{(J)}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\right] =Kπ,\displaystyle=K_{\pi}, 𝔼⁡[C~π(J)∣ℱn]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{C}_{\pi}^{(J)}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\right] =Cπ.\displaystyle=C_{\pi}. (41)

Because both coefficient maps are linear in the intervention-integrated right-hand side,

𝔼⁡[h~π,full,J∣ℱn]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{full},J}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\right] =h^π,full,\displaystyle=\widehat{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{full}}, 𝔼⁡[h~π,Nys,J∣ℱn]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{Nys},J}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\right] =h^π,Nys.\displaystyle=\widehat{h}_{\pi,\mathrm{Nys}}. (42)

The corresponding Hilbert-space Monte Carlo error is analyzed in Appendix D.

For fixed representation, kernels, and adjustment variables, the landmark set, matrices C,WC,W, and factorization of C⊤​C+n​λ​WC^{\top}C+n\lambda W are shared across interventions. Intervention integrals and intervention-specific density ratios are recomputed as needed.

Thus, evaluating a new supported intervention does not require refitting the conditional mean embedding. It requires only the intervention-specific policy integrals, density-ratio evaluations, and the resulting linear-system right-hand side.

B.4 Plug-in and inverse-probability variants

Our benchmark tables also compare two single-nuisance IMMD variants. For the finite-JJ projected construction, the plug-in, inverse-probability-weighted (IPW), and doubly robust coefficient vectors are

v~PI,J\displaystyle\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{PI},J} :=1n​C​Gλ​C~π(J)​𝟏n,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}CG_{\lambda}\widetilde{C}_{\pi}^{(J)}\mathbf{1}_{n}, v~IPW\displaystyle\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{IPW}} :=1n​𝒘^,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}\widehat{\bm{w}},
v~DR,J\displaystyle\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{DR},J} :=v~PI,J+1n​(𝒘^−C​Gλ​C⊤​𝒘^).\displaystyle:=\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{PI},J}+\frac{1}{n}\left(\widehat{\bm{w}}-CG_{\lambda}C^{\top}\widehat{\bm{w}}\right).

Thus, Plug-in–IMMD uses only the fitted conditional mean embedding, IPW–IMMD uses only the estimated policy ratio, and DR–IMMD combines both. The displayed IPW vector is the Horvitz–Thompson form; any declared benchmark-specific unit-mass rescaling is applied after these raw coefficients are constructed. For e∈{PI,IPW,DR}e\in\{\mathrm{PI},\mathrm{IPW},\mathrm{DR}\}, let v~e\widetilde{v}_{e} denote the corresponding vector above, with its JJ subscript suppressed. We freeze h~π,e=∑i=1nv~e,i​φ​(Zi)\widetilde{h}_{\pi,e}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widetilde{v}_{e,i}\varphi(Z_{i}) and apply the same particle flow. Hence the variants differ only in the target coefficients supplied to the optimizer.

B.5 Computational complexity

We compare the time and memory costs of the full-ridge and input-projected Nyström target constructions. Table 3 summarizes the comparison, while the discussion below details the dominant operations and the computations that can be reused across interventions.

For the full-ridge estimator, constructing and factorizing the n×nn\times n Gram system costs O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) time and O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) memory. When intervention integrals are approximated with JJ draws per context, forming the intervention-integrated right-hand side costs O⁡(J​n2)O(Jn^{2}); the remaining matrix–vector operations cost O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}).

For the Nyström estimator, forming C⊤​CC^{\top}C costs O⁡(n​mL2)O(nm_{L}^{2}), factorizing the resulting mL×mLm_{L}\times m_{L} system costs O⁡(mL3)O(m_{L}^{3}), and storing CC and WW requires O⁡(n​mL+mL2)O(nm_{L}+m_{L}^{2}) memory. Finite-JJ intervention integration costs O⁡(J​mL​n)O(Jm_{L}n), while constructing the remaining intervention-specific right-hand side and coefficients costs O⁡(n​mL+mL2)O(nm_{L}+m_{L}^{2}). For fixed JJ, the total target-construction cost is therefore O⁡(n​mL2+mL3)O(nm_{L}^{2}+m_{L}^{3}) time and O⁡(n​mL+mL2)O(nm_{L}+m_{L}^{2}) memory, assuming lazy or blockwise kernel evaluation. Precomputing the full Gram matrix would restore quadratic storage.

Input-side Nyström approximation reduces the cost of conditional-embedding regression and target construction, but it does not reduce the number of logged outcome features in the final target expansion. Consequently, direct evaluation of the target contribution for MM particles still costs O⁡(M​n)O(Mn) kernel gradients per particle iteration. Reducing this term would require an additional output-side approximation.

If the intervention integrals are available analytically, the factors proportional to JJ disappear. Moreover, the regression factorizations are reusable across supported interventions, so subsequent targets require only the intervention-specific integration and density-ratio computations.

The statistical guarantees in Appendix D require the landmark count mLm_{L} to increase with nn according to the leverage-based schedule stated there. A fixed landmark budget is therefore a computational approximation, rather than a general asymptotic consistency guarantee.

Appendix D Theoretical Analysis

D.1 Projected Nyström approximation of the conditional mean embedding

This section controls the error introduced when the conditional mean embedding nuisance is estimated by input-projected Nyström kernel ridge regression. The argument specializes the vector-valued regression analysis of El Ahmad et al. [17] to our setting. In contrast to their general construction, we sketch only the input RKHS. The latent-output RKHS remains unchanged, so no output-projection approximation term appears.

Statistical setup. Let 𝒮:=𝒜×𝒳,S:=(A,X),Z:=E⁡(Y),\mathcal{S}:=\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{X},\kern 5.0ptS:=(A,X),\kern 5.0ptZ:=E(Y), where the encoder EE is fixed and trained independently of the observations used in this section. Let (Si,Zi)i=1n(S_{i},Z_{i})_{i=1}^{n} be i.i.d. observations from the logged joint law P0P_{0}.

Let kS:𝒮×𝒮→ℝk_{S}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R} be a measurable positive-definite input kernel with RKHS ℋS\mathcal{H}_{S} and canonical feature map

φS​(s):=kS​(s,⋅).\varphi_{S}(s):=k_{S}(s,\cdot).

Let kZ:𝒵×𝒵→ℝk_{Z}:\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} be the positive-definite latent kernel used to define the interventional embedding, with RKHS ℋZ\mathcal{H}_{Z} and feature map

φZ​(z):=kZ​(z,⋅).\varphi_{Z}(z):=k_{Z}(z,\cdot).
Assumption D.1 (Measurability and kernel regularity).

We assume that

  • •

    The context, action, and latent spaces 𝒳\mathcal{X}, 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} are Polish spaces, equipped with their Borel σ\sigma-fields.

  • •

    The RKHSs ℋS\mathcal{H}_{S} and ℋZ\mathcal{H}_{Z} are separable, their feature maps are strongly measurable, and the fitted functions, operators, and displayed norms are measurable.

  • •

    There exist finite constants κS,κZ>0\kappa_{S},\kappa_{Z}>0 such that

    sups∈𝒮kS​(s,s)≤κS2,supz∈𝒵kZ​(z,z)≤κZ2.\sup_{s\in\mathcal{S}}k_{S}(s,s)\leq\kappa_{S}^{2},\qquad\sup_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}k_{Z}(z,z)\leq\kappa_{Z}^{2}.

Define the latent conditional mean embedding

m0​(s):=𝔼P0​[φZ​(Z)∣S=s]∈ℋZ.m_{0}(s):=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\!\left[\varphi_{Z}(Z)\mid S=s\right]\in\mathcal{H}_{Z}.

We use the identity-decomposable operator-valued kernel (OVK)

𝐊⁡(s,s′)=kS​(s,s′)​IℋZ.\mathbf{K}(s,s^{\prime})=k_{S}(s,s^{\prime})I_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}.

Its vector-valued RKHS is isometrically identified with the space 𝒮2​(ℋS,ℋZ)\mathcal{S}_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{S},\mathcal{H}_{Z}) of Hilbert–Schmidt operators: an operator H:ℋS→ℋZH:\mathcal{H}_{S}\to\mathcal{H}_{Z} represents the function

mH​(s)=H​φS​(s),‖mH‖𝒢=‖H‖HS.m_{H}(s)=H\varphi_{S}(s),\qquad\|m_{H}\|_{\mathcal{G}}=\|H\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.
Assumption D.2 (Attainability; El Ahmad et al. [17, Assumption 1]).

There exists H0∈𝒮2​(ℋS,ℋZ)H_{0}\in\mathcal{S}_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{S},\mathcal{H}_{Z}) such that

m0​(s)=H0​φS​(s)PS,0​-almost surely.m_{0}(s)=H_{0}\varphi_{S}(s)\qquad P_{S,0}\text{-almost surely}.

We now define the covariance operators associated with conditional mean embedding learning.

Definition D.3 (Population covariance operators).

Let PS,0P_{S,0} denote the marginal distribution of S=(A,X)S=(A,X) under the logging law. We define the population input covariance operator

CS:=𝔼P0​[φS​(S)⊗φS​(S)]:ℋS→ℋS,C_{S}:=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\varphi_{S}(S)\otimes\varphi_{S}(S)\right]:\mathcal{H}_{S}\to\mathcal{H}_{S},

and the population output–input cross-covariance operator

CZ​S:=𝔼P0​[φZ​(Z)⊗φS​(S)]:ℋS→ℋZ.C_{ZS}:=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}\left[\varphi_{Z}(Z)\otimes\varphi_{S}(S)\right]:\mathcal{H}_{S}\to\mathcal{H}_{Z}.

Under Assumption D.1, these Bochner expectations are well defined. The operator CSC_{S} is positive, self-adjoint, and trace class, with

Tr⁡(CS)=𝔼​‖φS​(S)‖ℋS2≤κS2.\operatorname{Tr}(C_{S})=\mathbb{E}\|\varphi_{S}(S)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}^{2}\leq\kappa_{S}^{2}.

Moreover, CZ​SC_{ZS} is Hilbert–Schmidt, since

‖φZ​(Z)⊗φS​(S)‖HS=‖φZ​(Z)‖ℋZ​‖φS​(S)‖ℋS≤κZ​κS.\|\varphi_{Z}(Z)\otimes\varphi_{S}(S)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}=\|\varphi_{Z}(Z)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}\|\varphi_{S}(S)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\leq\kappa_{Z}\kappa_{S}.
Lemma D.4 (Consequences of attainability).

Under Assumption D.2,

CZ​S=H0​CS.C_{ZS}=H_{0}C_{S}.

Moreover, for every H∈𝒮2​(ℋS,ℋZ)H\in\mathcal{S}_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{S},\mathcal{H}_{Z}),

‖mH−m0‖L2​(PS,0,ℋZ)=‖(H−H0)​CS1/2‖HS.\|m_{H}-m_{0}\|_{L_{2}(P_{S,0};\mathcal{H}_{Z})}=\|(H-H_{0})C_{S}^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}.
Proof.

For every f∈ℋSf\in\mathcal{H}_{S}, conditional expectation gives

CZ​S​f\displaystyle C_{ZS}f =𝔼⁡[φZ​(Z)​⟨φS​(S),f⟩ℋS]=𝔼⁡[m0​(S)​⟨φS​(S),f⟩ℋS]=H0​𝔼​[φS​(S)​⟨φS​(S),f⟩ℋS]=H0​CS​f.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi_{Z}(Z)\langle\varphi_{S}(S),f\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[m_{0}(S)\langle\varphi_{S}(S),f\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right]=H_{0}\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi_{S}(S)\langle\varphi_{S}(S),f\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right]=H_{0}C_{S}f.

This proves CZ​S=H0​CSC_{ZS}=H_{0}C_{S}. For the second statement,

‖mH−m0‖L2​(PS,0,ℋZ)2\displaystyle\|m_{H}-m_{0}\|_{L_{2}(P_{S,0};\mathcal{H}_{Z})}^{2} =𝔼⁡[‖(H−H0)​φS​(S)‖ℋZ2]=Tr⁡[(H−H0)​CS​(H−H0)∗]=‖(H−H0)​CS1/2‖HS2.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\|(H-H_{0})\varphi_{S}(S)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}^{2}\right]=\operatorname{Tr}\left[(H-H_{0})C_{S}(H-H_{0})^{*}\right]=\|(H-H_{0})C_{S}^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}.

Taking nonnegative square roots completes the proof. ∎

The next assumption characterizes the eigendecay of the input covariance operator and the maximal leverage of the input features. These quantities determine how many uniformly sampled landmarks are sufficient for the projected Nyström estimator to retain the statistical accuracy of full kernel ridge regression.

Assumption D.5 (Input spectral regularity; El Ahmad et al. [17, Assumption 3-4]).

For some γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1],

QS:=Tr⁡(CSγ)<∞.Q_{S}:=\operatorname{Tr}(C_{S}^{\gamma})<\infty.

Moreover, for some μ∈[0,1)\mu\in[0,1) and BS<∞B_{S}<\infty, we have φS​(s)⊗φS​(s)⪯BS​CS1−μ​PS,0​-almost surely.\varphi_{S}(s)\otimes\varphi_{S}(s)\preceq B_{S}C_{S}^{1-\mu}\kern 5.0ptP_{S,0}\text{-almost surely}.

Definition D.6 (Empirical sampling and covariance operators).

Given observations (Si,Zi)i=1n,(S_{i},Z_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, define the normalized sampling operators

𝖳S\displaystyle\mathsf{T}_{S} :ℋS→ℝn,\displaystyle:\mathcal{H}_{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, (𝖳S​f)i\displaystyle(\mathsf{T}_{S}f)_{i} :=1nf(Si),𝖳Z:ℋZ→ℝn,\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}f(S_{i}),\quad\mathsf{T}_{Z}:\mathcal{H}_{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, (𝖳Z​g)i:=1n​g​(Zi).\displaystyle(\mathsf{T}_{Z}g)_{i}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}g(Z_{i}). (47)

With ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} equipped with its standard Euclidean inner product, their adjoints are

𝖳S∗​a\displaystyle\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}a =1n∑i=1naiφS(Si),𝖳Z∗a=1n∑i=1naiφZ(Zi),a∈ℝn.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\varphi_{S}(S_{i}),\quad\mathsf{T}_{Z}^{*}a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i}),\quad a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. (48)

The empirical input covariance and output–input cross-covariance operators are respectively

C^S\displaystyle\widehat{C}_{S} :=𝖳S∗𝖳S=1n∑i=1nφS(Si)⊗φS(Si),C^Z​S:=𝖳Z∗𝖳S=1n∑i=1nφZ(Zi)⊗φS(Si).\displaystyle:=\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\mathsf{T}_{S}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varphi_{S}(S_{i})\otimes\varphi_{S}(S_{i}),\quad\widehat{C}_{ZS}:=\mathsf{T}_{Z}^{*}\mathsf{T}_{S}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i})\otimes\varphi_{S}(S_{i}). (49)

Dense Hilbert-valued ridge regression. By Definition D.6, for every H∈𝒮2​(ℋS,ℋZ)H\in\mathcal{S}_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{S},\mathcal{H}_{Z}),

‖𝖳Z∗−H​𝖳S∗‖HS2\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathsf{T}_{Z}^{*}-H\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2} =1n​∑i=1n‖φZ​(Zi)−H​φS​(Si)‖ℋZ2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lVert\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i})-H\varphi_{S}(S_{i})\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}^{2}. (50)

Consequently, for λ>0\lambda>0, the dense empirical ridge estimator is defined by

H^λ∈arg​minH∈𝒮2​(ℋS,ℋZ)⁡{‖𝖳Z∗−H​𝖳S∗‖HS2+λ​‖H‖HS2}.\displaystyle\widehat{H}_{\lambda}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{H\in\mathcal{S}_{2}(\mathcal{H}_{S},\mathcal{H}_{Z})}\left\{\left\lVert\mathsf{T}_{Z}^{*}-H\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert H\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\right\}. (51)

Let KS:=(kS​(Si,Sj))i,j=1n∈ℝn×n,K_{S}:=\bigl(k_{S}(S_{i},S_{j})\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, and, for s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, define kS​(s):=(kS​(Si,s))i=1n∈ℝn.k_{S}(s):=\bigl(k_{S}(S_{i},s)\bigr)_{i=1}^{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. For the product kernel introduced in the algorithmic section, KS=KA​XK_{S}=K_{AX}.

Proposition D.7 (Dense Hilbert-valued ridge solution; [44, Theorem (4.1)], [17, Equation (3)-(4)]).

The optimization problem equation 51 admits a unique minimizer, given by

H^λ\displaystyle\widehat{H}_{\lambda} =C^Z​S​(C^S+λ​IℋS)−1.\displaystyle=\widehat{C}_{ZS}\left(\widehat{C}_{S}+\lambda I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right)^{-1}. (52)

Consequently, writing m^λ​(s):=H^λ​φS​(s),\widehat{m}_{\lambda}(s):=\widehat{H}_{\lambda}\varphi_{S}(s), we have the equivalent representer formula

m^λ​(s)\displaystyle\widehat{m}_{\lambda}(s) =∑i=1n[(KS+n​λ​In)−1​kS​(s)]i​φZ​(Zi).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\left(K_{S}+n\lambda I_{n}\right)^{-1}k_{S}(s)\right]_{i}\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i}). (53)

Generic input sketch and Nyström specialization.

Following El Ahmad et al. [17], let 𝖱∈ℝm×n\mathsf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be a a possibly random input-sketch matrix. El Ahmad et al. [17] formulate their method for general input and output sketches; here we sketch only the input RKHS and leave the latent-output RKHS unchanged.

Define the input-sketch operator and its adjoint

𝖡R\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{R} :=𝖱𝖳S:ℋS→ℝm,𝖡R∗=𝖳S∗​𝖱⊤:ℝm→ℋS,\displaystyle:=\mathsf{R}\mathsf{T}_{S}:{\mathcal{H}}_{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{m},\quad\mathsf{B}_{R}^{*}=\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\mathsf{R}^{\top}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{S}, (54)

The input-sketch operator induces the finite dimensional subspace

ℋS,R≔Range⁡(𝖡R∗)⊆ℋ𝒮.{\mathcal{H}}_{S,R}\coloneqq\operatorname{Range}(\mathsf{B}_{R}^{*})\subseteq{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{S}}.

To make this explicit, let eje_{j} denote the jj-th canonical basis vector of ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}. Then,

𝖡R∗​ej=1n​∑i=1n𝖱j​i​φ𝒮​(Si).\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{R}^{*}e_{j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathsf{R}_{ji}\varphi_{\mathcal{S}}(S_{i}).

Consequently,

ℋS,R\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{S,R} =span{∑i=1nRj​iφS(Si):j=1,…,m}.\displaystyle=\operatorname{span}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}R_{ji}\varphi_{S}(S_{i}):j=1,\ldots,m\right\}.

The orthogonal projector onto this subspace is

PR:=𝖡R∗​(𝖡R​𝖡R∗)†​𝖡R,\displaystyle P_{R}:=\mathsf{B}_{R}^{*}(\mathsf{B}_{R}\mathsf{B}_{R}^{*})^{\dagger}\mathsf{B}_{R}, (55)

where †\dagger denotes Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. To verify the projector formula, let rR=rank⁡(𝖡R)r_{R}=\operatorname{rank}(\mathsf{B}_{R}) and consider the reduced singular value decomposition

𝖡R=UR​ΣR​VR∗,\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{R}=U_{R}\Sigma_{R}V_{R}^{*},

where UR:ℝrR→ℝmU_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{r_{R}}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} and VR:ℝrR→ℋSV_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{r_{R}}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{S} are isometries, and ΣR\Sigma_{R} is diagonal with strictly positive entries. Then PR=VR​VR∗P_{R}=V_{R}V_{R}^{*}.

For the Nyström estimator used here, choose 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n, draw distinct landmark indices

L={ℓ1,…,ℓm}⊆{1,…,n}\displaystyle L=\{\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m}\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}

uniformly without replacement [53], and define the coordinate-selection matrix 𝖱L∈ℝm×n\mathsf{R}_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} defined, for a∈ℝna\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, by

(𝖱La)j=aℓj,j=1,…,m.\displaystyle(\mathsf{R}_{L}a)_{j}=a_{\ell_{j}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.

Next, define the landmark synthesis operator as

ΦL:ℝm→ℋS,ΦL​c=∑j=1mcj​φS​(Sℓj).\displaystyle\Phi_{L}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to{\mathcal{H}}_{S},\quad\Phi_{L}c=\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{j}\varphi_{S}(S_{\ell_{j}}).

Its adjoint is the landmark evaluation operator given by

ΦL∗​f=[f⁡(Sℓ1)f⁡(Sℓm)]∈ℝm\displaystyle\Phi_{L}^{*}f=\begin{bmatrix}f(S_{\ell_{1}})\\ \vdots\\ f(S_{\ell_{m}})\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}

The normalized sampling operator and the landmark synthesis operator are related by

𝖱L​𝖳S\displaystyle\mathsf{R}_{L}\mathsf{T}_{S} =1n​ΦL∗,𝖳S∗​𝖱L⊤=1n​ΦL,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Phi_{L}^{*},\quad\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\mathsf{R}_{L}^{\top}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Phi_{L},

Consequently, the subspace induced by the Nyström sketch is

ℋS,RL=Range⁡(𝖳S∗​𝖱L⊤)=Range⁡(ΦL)=span⁡{φS​(Sℓ):ℓ∈L}.\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{S,R_{L}}=\operatorname{Range}(\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\mathsf{R}_{L}^{\top})=\operatorname{Range}(\Phi_{L})=\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{S}(S_{\ell}):\ell\in L\}.

Thus the Nyström approximation restricts the dependence of the conditional mean embedding to the span of the landmark input features. Define the landmark Gram matrix W:=ΦL∗​ΦLW:=\Phi_{L}^{*}\Phi_{L} with entries given by Wj​r=⟨φ𝒮​(Sℓj),φ⁡(Sℓr)⟩ℋ𝒮=k𝒮​(Sℓj,Sℓr).W_{jr}=\langle\varphi_{\mathcal{S}}(S_{\ell_{j}}),\varphi(S_{\ell_{r}})\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{S}}}=k_{\mathcal{S}}(S_{\ell_{j}},S_{\ell_{r}}). Hence,

W=𝖱L​KS​𝖱L⊤=KS​[L,L]∈ℝm×m.W=\mathsf{R}_{L}K_{S}\mathsf{R}_{L}^{\top}=K_{S}[L,L]\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}.

The generic sketch projector now becomes

PL=PRL=ΦL​W†​ΦL∗.\displaystyle P_{L}=P_{R_{L}}=\Phi_{L}W^{\dagger}\Phi_{L}^{*}. (56)

Projected regression problem. The sketch projector PRP_{R} decomposes the input RKHS as

ℋ𝒮=ℋ𝒮,R⊕ℋ𝒮,R⟂,ℋ𝒮,R=Range⁡(PR).\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{S}}={\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathcal{S}},R}\oplus{\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathcal{S}},R}^{\perp},\quad{\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathcal{S}},R}=\operatorname{Range}(P_{R}).

We restrict the regression operator to use only the component of the input feature lying in ℋ𝒮,R.{\mathcal{H}}_{{\mathcal{S}},R}. Define the restricted operator class

𝒮2,R:={H∈𝒮⁡(ℋ𝒮,ℋ𝒵):H=H​PR}.\displaystyle{\mathcal{S}}_{2,R}:=\left\{H\in{\mathcal{S}}({\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{S}},{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{Z}}):H=HP_{R}\right\}.

The condition H=H​PRH=HP_{R} is equivalent to H⁡(Iℋ𝒮−PR)=0H(I_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{S}}}-P_{R})=0. Thus, HH annihilates all the input directions orthogonal to the sketch-induced subspace. For the associated regression function, we have

mH​(s)=H​φS​(s)=H​PR​φS​(s).m_{H}(s)=H\varphi_{S}(s)=HP_{R}\varphi_{S}(s).

Therefore, the estimator depends on ss only through the projected feature PR​φ𝒮​(s)P_{R}\varphi_{\mathcal{S}}(s). The corresponding input-sketched vector-valued function class is

𝒢R:={mH:mH(s)=HφS(s),H∈𝒮2,R}.\displaystyle{\mathcal{G}}_{R}:=\left\{m_{H}:m_{H}(s)=H\varphi_{S}(s),\ H\in{\mathcal{S}}_{2,R}\right\}.

Next, we define the input-sketched ridge estimator by

H^R,λ∈arg​minH∈𝒮2,R⁡{‖𝖳Z∗−H​𝖳S∗‖HS2+λ​‖H‖HS2}.\displaystyle\widehat{H}_{R,\lambda}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\in\mathcal{S}_{2,R}\end{subarray}}\left\{\left\lVert\mathsf{T}_{Z}^{*}-H\mathsf{T}_{S}^{*}\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert H\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\right\}. (57)

Equivalently,

H^R,λ∈arg​minH∈𝒮2​(ℋS,ℋZ)H=H​PR⁡{1n​∑i=1n‖φ𝒵​(Zi)−H​PR​φ𝒮​(Si)‖ℋ𝒵2+λ​‖H‖HS2}.\displaystyle\widehat{H}_{R,\lambda}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\in\mathcal{S}_{2}({\mathcal{H}}_{S},{\mathcal{H}}_{Z})\\ H=HP_{R}\end{subarray}}\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lVert\varphi_{\mathcal{Z}}(Z_{i})-HP_{R}\varphi_{\mathcal{S}}(S_{i})\right\rVert_{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathcal{Z}}}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert H\right\rVert_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2}\right\}. (58)

It is ordinary Hilbert-valued ridge regression after replacing each input feature φ𝒮​(Si)\varphi_{\mathcal{S}}(S_{i}) by its projection onto the sketched subspace. This estimator is the input-only sketching specialization of the low-rank Hilbert-valued estimator of El Ahmad et al. [17, Section 3 and Appendix C, Lemma 1, Equations (29)–(34)]. For Nyström row selection, this is the Hilbert-valued analogue of the landmark-subspace estimator of Rudi et al. [53, Section 2, Eqs. (3)–(5)].

Recall that rR=rank⁡(𝖡R)r_{R}=\operatorname{rank}(\mathsf{B}_{R}) and that the reduced singular value decomposition of the sketching operator is 𝖡R=UR​ΣR​VR∗,\mathsf{B}_{R}=U_{R}\Sigma_{R}V_{R}^{*}, where VR:ℝrR→ℋSV_{R}:\mathbb{R}^{r_{R}}\to\mathcal{H}_{S} is an isometry satisfying VR∗​VR=IrR, and ​VR​VR∗=PR.V_{R}^{*}V_{R}=I_{r_{R}},\text{ and }V_{R}V_{R}^{*}=P_{R}. Hence the columns of VRV_{R} form an orthonormal basis of the sketch-induced subspace ℋS,R=Range⁡(PR).\mathcal{H}_{S,R}=\operatorname{Range}(P_{R}). In particular, every f∈ℋS,Rf\in\mathcal{H}_{S,R} admits the unique representation

f=VR​a,a=VR∗​f∈ℝrR.f=V_{R}a,\qquad a=V_{R}^{*}f\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{R}}.

We define the reduced empirical covariance matrix by

C^S,Rred:=VR∗​C^S​VR∈ℝrR×rR.\widehat{C}_{S,R}^{\mathrm{red}}:=V_{R}^{*}\widehat{C}_{S}V_{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{R}\times r_{R}}. (59)

This matrix is the coordinate representation of the empirical covariance operator C^S\widehat{C}_{S} on the sketched subspace. Indeed, for every a∈ℝrRa\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{R}},

a⊤​C^S,Rred​a\displaystyle a^{\top}\widehat{C}_{S,R}^{\mathrm{red}}a =⟨VR​a,C^S​VR​a⟩ℋS=1n​∑i=1n|⟨VR​a,φS​(Si)⟩ℋS|2≥0.\displaystyle=\left\langle V_{R}a,\widehat{C}_{S}V_{R}a\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\left\langle V_{R}a,\varphi_{S}(S_{i})\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right|^{2}\geq 0.

Thus C^S,Rred\widehat{C}_{S,R}^{\mathrm{red}} is symmetric and positive semi-definite. Consequently, for every λ>0\lambda>0, C^S,Rred+λ​IrR⪰λ​IrR,\widehat{C}_{S,R}^{\mathrm{red}}+\lambda I_{r_{R}}\succeq\lambda I_{r_{R}}, and the regularized reduced covariance is invertible.

Definition D.8 (Restricted regularized inverse).

Following El Ahmad et al. [17, Lemma 1, Equation (29)], define the restricted regularized inverse for λ>0\lambda>0

ηR,λ​(C^S):=VR​(C^S,Rred+λ​IrR)−1​VR∗:ℋS→ℋS.\eta_{R,\lambda}(\widehat{C}_{S}):=V_{R}\left(\widehat{C}_{S,R}^{\mathrm{red}}+\lambda I_{r_{R}}\right)^{-1}V_{R}^{*}:\mathcal{H}_{S}\to\mathcal{H}_{S}. (60)

The following result is the input-only specialization of El Ahmad et al. [17, Appendix C, Lemma 1, Eq. (29), with the derivation in Eqs. (31)–(34)].

Proposition D.9 (Projected Hilbert-valued ridge solution).

The optimization problem equation 57 admits a unique minimizer, given by

H^R,λ=C^Z​S​ηR,λ​(C^S).\widehat{H}_{R,\lambda}=\widehat{C}_{ZS}\eta_{R,\lambda}(\widehat{C}_{S}). (61)

Moreover, the restricted inverse satisfies

PR​(C^S+λ​IℋS)​ηR,λ​(C^S)\displaystyle P_{R}\left(\widehat{C}_{S}+\lambda I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right)\eta_{R,\lambda}(\widehat{C}_{S}) =PR,\displaystyle=P_{R}, (62)
ηR,λ​(C^S)​(C^S+λ​IℋS)​PR\displaystyle\eta_{R,\lambda}(\widehat{C}_{S})\left(\widehat{C}_{S}+\lambda I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right)P_{R} =PR.\displaystyle=P_{R}. (63)

The purpose of ηR,λ​(C^S)\eta_{R,\lambda}(\widehat{C}_{S}) is not only to express the projected estimator compactly. It will also isolate the effect of restricting the regression to the sketch-induced input subspace. In the subsequent error decomposition, the estimator is compared with the population regression operator through a sample term, a projection term, and a population ridge-bias term. The inverse identities above are the main algebraic tool used to control the projection contribution.

Population ridge comparison. From this point onward, we specialize the generic sketch to the Nyström landmark sketch RLR_{L}, and write

PL:=PRL,ηL,λ:=ηRL,λ​(C^S).P_{L}:=P_{R_{L}},\qquad\eta_{L,\lambda}:=\eta_{R_{L},\lambda}(\widehat{C}_{S}).
