H^L,λ=C^Z​S​ηL,λ,m^L,λ​(s):=H^L,λ​φS​(s).\widehat{H}_{L,\lambda}=\widehat{C}_{ZS}\eta_{L,\lambda},\qquad\widehat{m}_{L,\lambda}(s):=\widehat{H}_{L,\lambda}\varphi_{S}(s).

Since CSC_{S} is positive and self-adjoint, CS,λ⪰λ​IℋS.C_{S,\lambda}\succeq\lambda I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}. It is therefore boundedly invertible, with ‖CS,λ−1‖op≤λ−1.\|C_{S,\lambda}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\lambda^{-1}.

Following the input-only specialization of El Ahmad et al. [17, Appendix D, proof of Theorem 1, Eqs. (43)–(48)], we introduce the following comparison operator and error decomposition.

Lemma D.10 (Projected Nyström error decomposition).

Suppose Assumptions D.1 and D.2 hold. For λ>0\lambda>0, let CS,λ:=CS+λ​IℋS,C_{S,\lambda}:=C_{S}+\lambda I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}, and define Hλ:=H0​CS​CS,λ−1.H_{\lambda}:=H_{0}C_{S}C_{S,\lambda}^{-1}. Then

Consequently,

rm​(L,λ):=‖m^L,λ−m0‖L2​(PS,0,ℋZ)≤(A)L,λ+(B)L,λ+(C)λ,r_{m}(L,\lambda):=\left\|\widehat{m}_{L,\lambda}-m_{0}\right\|_{L_{2}(P_{S,0};\mathcal{H}_{Z})}\leq(A)_{L,\lambda}+(B)_{L,\lambda}+(C)_{\lambda}, (66)

where

(A)L,λ\displaystyle(A)_{L,\lambda} :=‖(C^Z​S−Hλ​C^S)​ηL,λ​CS1/2‖HS,\displaystyle:=\left\|\left(\widehat{C}_{ZS}-H_{\lambda}\widehat{C}_{S}\right)\eta_{L,\lambda}C_{S}^{1/2}\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}},
(B)L,λ\displaystyle(B)_{L,\lambda} :=‖Hλ​(C^S​ηL,λ−IℋS)​CS1/2‖HS,\displaystyle:=\left\|H_{\lambda}\left(\widehat{C}_{S}\eta_{L,\lambda}-I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}\right)C_{S}^{1/2}\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}},
(C)λ\displaystyle(C)_{\lambda} :=‖(Hλ−H0)​CS1/2‖HS.\displaystyle:=\left\|\left(H_{\lambda}-H_{0}\right)C_{S}^{1/2}\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}. (67)
Proof.

Since CS​CS,λ−1=IℋS−λ​CS,λ−1,C_{S}C_{S,\lambda}^{-1}=I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}-\lambda C_{S,\lambda}^{-1}, Equation 64 follows immediately. Using H^L,λ=C^Z​S​ηL,λ,\widehat{H}_{L,\lambda}=\widehat{C}_{ZS}\eta_{L,\lambda}, add and subtract Hλ​C^S​ηL,λH_{\lambda}\widehat{C}_{S}\eta_{L,\lambda} and HλH_{\lambda} to obtain Equation 65. The prediction-norm identity in Lemma D.4, followed by the triangle inequality, yields Equation 66. ∎

Lemma D.10 gives an exact algebraic decomposition of the projected Nyström estimation error into three components, which will be controlled separately. Because the decomposition holds pathwise for every realized sample and landmark set, it does not yet require the input-capacity or embedding assumptions, uniform landmark sampling, or concentration arguments. The sample term (A)L,λ(A)_{L,\lambda} captures fluctuations in the empirical covariance and cross-covariance operators. The projection/resolvent term (B)L,λ(B)_{L,\lambda} quantifies the error induced by restricting the regression to the landmark subspace and using the associated restricted regularized inverse. Finally, (C)λ(C)_{\lambda} is the deterministic bias introduced by population ridge regularization. The additional assumptions enter only when deriving bounds for these three terms.

C^S,λ:=C^S+λ​IℋS.\widehat{C}_{S,\lambda}:=\widehat{C}_{S}+\lambda I_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}.

The following lemma is the input-only counterpart of El Ahmad et al. [17, Lemma 5, Eqs. (74)–(81)]. Because the output RKHS is not sketched, their output-projection term vanishes. We use a direct spectral calculation to obtain a slightly sharper constant.

Lemma D.13 (Population ridge bias).

For every λ>0\lambda>0,

(C)λ≤λ2​‖H0‖HS.(C)_{\lambda}\leq\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{2}\|H_{0}\|_{\mathrm{HS}}. (75)

Reduction to the Nyström projection error. Combining Lemmas D.11, D.12, and D.13, we obtain, on ℰcmp​(λ)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cmp}}(\lambda),

It remains to control the random subspace error εL\varepsilon_{L} defined in equation 70.

For λ>0\lambda>0, define the effective dimension

𝒩⁡(λ):=Tr⁡[CS​CS,λ−1],\mathcal{N}(\lambda):=\operatorname{Tr}\left[C_{S}C_{S,\lambda}^{-1}\right], (77)

𝒩∞​(λ):=ess​sups∼PS,0⁡⟨φS​(s),CS,λ−1​φS​(s)⟩ℋS.\mathcal{N}_{\infty}(\lambda):=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{s\sim P_{S,0}}\left\langle\varphi_{S}(s),C_{S,\lambda}^{-1}\varphi_{S}(s)\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{S}}. (78)

Lemma D.14 (Uniform Nyström projection control).

Let L⊆{1,…,n}L\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} contain mm indices sampled uniformly without replacement, and let PLP_{L} be the orthogonal projector onto

Same-sample embedding estimation.

We next verify the outcome-side class control needed when the regression and the DR score use the same observations. All asymptotic statements below use the same ridge and landmark sequences, with the finite-sample conditions of Theorem D.16 holding eventually for each fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1).

Lemma D.20 (Smooth parametric weights).

Retain the identification, kernel, fixed-policy, weight-moment, and outcome-operator conditions of Proposition D.19, and suppose ‖m^−m0‖L2​(PS,0,ℋZ)=oℙ​(1)\|\widehat{m}-m_{0}\|_{L_{2}(P_{S,0};\mathcal{H}_{Z})}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1). Replace its ratio-RKHS conditions by w^=wθ^\widehat{w}=w_{\widehat{\theta}}, wθ0=w0w_{\theta_{0}}=w_{0}, where θ∈ℝp\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, pp is fixed, and ∥θ^−θ0∥2=Oℙ(n−1/2)\|\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0}\|_{2}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}). ‖w˙θ0‖2∈L2​(PS,0),B⁡(s):=supθ∈U‖w¨θ​(s)‖op∈L2​(PS,0).\|\dot{w}_{\theta_{0}}\|_{2}\in L_{2}(P_{S,0}),\qquad B(s):=\sup_{\theta\in U}\|\ddot{w}_{\theta}(s)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\in L_{2}(P_{S,0}).

∥w^−w0∥L2​(PS,0)=Oℙ(n−1/2),∥𝔾n(Γη^−Γ0)∥ℋZ=oℙ(1),\|\widehat{w}-w_{0}\|_{L_{2}(P_{S,0})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}),\qquad\|\mathbb{G}_{n}(\Gamma_{\widehat{\eta}}-\Gamma_{0})\|_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1),

and

h^π−χ(π)=(Pn−P0)Γ0+oℙ(n−1/2).\widehat{h}_{\pi}-\chi(\pi)=(P_{n}-P_{0})\Gamma_{0}+o_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}).
Proof.

Put Δn=θ^−θ0\Delta_{n}=\widehat{\theta}-\theta_{0}. On the event θ^∈U\widehat{\theta}\in U, whose probability tends to one, Taylor’s formula gives

qn=w˙θ0⊤​Δn+Rn,|Rn|≤12​B​‖Δn‖22.q_{n}=\dot{w}_{\theta_{0}}^{\top}\Delta_{n}+R_{n},\qquad|R_{n}|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}B\|\Delta_{n}\|_{2}^{2}.

The L2L_{2} assumptions imply the stated ratio rate. For any fixed bounded strongly measurable function cc taking values in a separable Hilbert space,

‖𝔾n​[qn​c]‖\displaystyle\|\mathbb{G}_{n}[q_{n}c]\| ≤‖Δn‖2​∑j=1p‖𝔾n​[w˙θ0,j​c]‖\displaystyle\leq\|\Delta_{n}\|_{2}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\|\mathbb{G}_{n}[\dot{w}_{\theta_{0},j}c]\|
+12n∥Δn∥22∥c∥∞(PnB+P0B)=Oℙ(n−1/2).\displaystyle\quad+\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{n}\|\Delta_{n}\|_{2}^{2}\|c\|_{\infty}(P_{n}B+P_{0}B)=O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}).

Here the fixed empirical processes have bounded second moments and Pn​B+P0​B=Oℙ​(1)P_{n}B+P_{0}B=O_{\mathbb{P}}(1). These are pathwise bounds and do not require independence between θ^\widehat{\theta} and the observations. Apply the bound to c=r0c=r_{0} and c=φSc=\varphi_{S} in equation 97. The outcome localization in Proposition D.19 handles its first term, while ‖H^−H0‖op=Oℙ​(1)\|\widehat{H}-H_{0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(1) controls the multiplier of the last term. Finally the ratio rate and outcome consistency make the product remainder in equation 95 oℙ(n−1/2)o_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}). ∎

A concrete sufficient model is Gaussian logging regression A|X∼𝒩⁡(B0​z​(X),Σ)A\mid X\sim\mathcal{N}(B_{0}z(X),\Sigma), with bounded regressors z⁡(X)z(X), nonsingular 𝔼⁡[z⁡(X)​z​(X)⊤]\mathbb{E}[z(X)z(X)^{\top}], and fixed known Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0. For a fixed target π(⋅∣X)=𝒩(μπ(X),Σ)\pi(\cdot\mid X)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\pi}(X),\Sigma) with bounded μπ\mu_{\pi}, take B^\widehat{B} to be ordinary least squares and wB=π/pBw_{B}=\pi/p_{B}. The regression coefficients are root-nn consistent. On a bounded neighbourhood of B0B_{0}, the ratio and its first two derivatives are bounded by a polynomial in ‖A‖\|A\| times exp⁡(C​‖A‖+C)\exp(C\|A\|+C) for a finite CC. Gaussian tails therefore verify the derivative envelopes and P0​w02<∞P_{0}w_{0}^{2}<\infty required above.

Lemma D.18 and equation 93 verify the outcome conditions for the projected estimator, including with landmarks selected from the same data. For the weights, Proposition D.19 gives RKHS sufficient conditions, and Lemma D.20 gives a smooth parametric alternative. Also, ‖Γ0‖≤κZ​(1+2​w0)\|\Gamma_{0}\|\leq\kappa_{Z}(1+2w_{0}) verifies the oracle second moment. Removing the product remainder from equation 96 additionally requires the product of nuisance errors to be oℙ(n−1/2)o_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}); the rate below needs only the weaker Oℙ​(1)O_{\mathbb{P}}(1) score control.

Corollary D.21 (Projected Nyström DR embedding rate).

Suppose Corollary D.17 holds and

‖w^−w0‖L2​(PS,0)=Oℙ​(rw,n).\|\widehat{w}-w_{0}\|_{L_{2}(P_{S,0})}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(r_{w,n}).

𝔼​‖Γm0,w0​(O)‖ℋZ2<∞\mathbb{E}\|\Gamma_{m_{0},w_{0}}(O)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}^{2}<\infty

and that

‖(Pn−P0){Γm^Ln,λn,w^−Γm0,w0}‖ℋZ=Oℙ(n−1/2).\left\|(P_{n}-P_{0})\left\{\Gamma_{\widehat{m}_{L_{n},\lambda_{n}},\widehat{w}}-\Gamma_{m_{0},w_{0}}\right\}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(n^{-1/2}).

These two score conditions hold under the fixed-policy and ratio conditions of Proposition D.19 or Lemma D.20, together with Lemma D.18; known weights require only P0​w02<∞P_{0}w_{0}^{2}<\infty. Then

‖χ^DR,Nys(π)−χ(π)‖ℋZ=Oℙ(n−1/2+rw,nn−12​(1+γ)).\left\|\widehat{\chi}_{\mathrm{DR,Nys}}(\pi)-\chi(\pi)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{Z}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{w,n}n^{-\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma)}}\right). (98)
Proof.

Apply equation 95, the Hilbert-valued Cauchy–Schwarz bound for the product remainder, and Corollary D.17. ∎

Finite target-policy Monte Carlo approximation.

The preceding results concern the projected Nyström doubly robust estimator defined using the exact target-policy integral. We now control the additional error induced by approximating this integral with J≥1J\geq 1 conditionally independent target-policy draws at each logged context, as in the continuous-action resampling construction of Zenati et al. [62].

Write

m^n:=m^Ln,λn,χ^n:=χ^DR,Nys​(π).\widehat{m}_{n}:=\widehat{m}_{L_{n},\lambda_{n}},\qquad\widehat{\chi}_{n}:=\widehat{\chi}_{\mathrm{DR,Nys}}(\pi).

Here, χ^n\widehat{\chi}_{n} denotes the theoretical projected Nyström estimator defined using the exact target-policy integral.

For every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, define the exact policy average

m¯n​(Xi):=∫𝒜m^n​(a,Xi)​π​(𝑑a∣Xi),\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i}):=\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})\,\pi(da\mid X_{i}), (99)

where the integral is a Bochner integral in ℋZ{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}. Its existence is ensured by the moment condition imposed in Lemma D.22. The exact-integral estimator can then be written as

χ^n\displaystyle\widehat{\chi}_{n} =1n​∑i=1n[w^​(Ai,Xi)​{φZ​(Zi)−m^n​(Ai,Xi)}+m¯n​(Xi)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigg[\widehat{w}(A_{i},X_{i})\left\{\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i})-\widehat{m}_{n}(A_{i},X_{i})\right\}+\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i})\Bigg]. (100)

Let ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} denote the sigma-field generated by all randomness used to construct m^n\widehat{m}_{n}, w^\widehat{w}, and χ^n\widehat{\chi}_{n} prior to drawing the target-policy Monte Carlo actions. In particular, ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n} contains the logged sample and the selected landmark set.

Conditional on ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n}, draw

Ai​uπ∣ℱn∼π(⋅∣Xi),i=1,…,n,u=1,…,J,A_{iu}^{\pi}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid X_{i}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\quad u=1,\ldots,J, (101)

independently across all pairs (i,u)(i,u). Define the Monte Carlo policy average

m¯n,J​(Xi):=1J​∑u=1Jm^n​(Ai​uπ,Xi),\overline{m}_{n,J}(X_{i}):=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{u=1}^{J}\widehat{m}_{n}(A_{iu}^{\pi},X_{i}), (102)

and the corresponding finite-JJ estimator

χ~n,J\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J} :=1n​∑i=1n[w^​(Ai,Xi)​{φZ​(Zi)−m^n​(Ai,Xi)}+m¯n,J​(Xi)].\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Bigg[\widehat{w}(A_{i},X_{i})\left\{\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i})-\widehat{m}_{n}(A_{i},X_{i})\right\}+\overline{m}_{n,J}(X_{i})\Bigg]. (103)

The exact and finite-JJ estimators differ only through the target-policy integration term:

χ~n,J−χ^n=1n​∑i=1n{m¯n,J​(Xi)−m¯n​(Xi)}.\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\overline{m}_{n,J}(X_{i})-\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i})\right\}. (104)

Using the same target-policy draws and the same projected regression subspace, χ~n,J\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J} coincides with

χ~DR,Nys,J​(π)\widetilde{\chi}_{\mathrm{DR,Nys},J}(\pi)

in the matrix notation of Appendix B.2.

Lemma D.22 (Finite-JJ policy-integration error).

Assume that, almost surely, for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, the map

a⟼m^n​(a,Xi)a\longmapsto\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})

is strongly measurable and satisfies

∫𝒜‖m^n​(a,Xi)‖ℋZ2​π​(𝑑a∣Xi)<∞.\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\left\|\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\pi(da\mid X_{i})<\infty. (105)

Define the conditional average policy variance

Vn:=1n​∑i=1n∫𝒜‖m^n​(a,Xi)−m¯n​(Xi)‖ℋZ2​π​(𝑑a∣Xi).V_{n}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\left\|\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})-\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i})\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\pi(da\mid X_{i}). (106)

Then, almost surely,

𝔼⁡[χ~n,J|ℱn]=χ^n,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right]=\widehat{\chi}_{n}, (107)

and

𝔼⁡[‖χ~n,J−χ^n‖ℋZ2|ℱn]=Vnn​J.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right]=\frac{V_{n}}{nJ}. (108)

Consequently, for every δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1),

Pr(‖χ~n,J−χ^n‖ℋZ>Vnn​J​δ|ℱn)≤δ.\Pr\!\left(\left.\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}>\sqrt{\frac{V_{n}}{nJ\delta}}\,\right|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right)\leq\delta. (109)
Proof.

For i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and u=1,…,Ju=1,\ldots,J, define

ξi​u:=m^n​(Ai​uπ,Xi)−m¯n​(Xi).\xi_{iu}:=\widehat{m}_{n}(A_{iu}^{\pi},X_{i})-\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i}).

By the definition of the exact policy average, 𝔼⁡[ξi​u|ℱn]=0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\xi_{iu}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right]=0. Moreover, conditionally on ℱn\mathcal{F}_{n}, the collection {ξi​u:i=1,…,n,u=1,…,J}\{\xi_{iu}:i=1,\ldots,n,\ u=1,\ldots,J\} is mutually independent.

Using equation 104, we have

χ~n,J−χ^n=1n​J​∑i=1n∑u=1Jξi​u.\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}=\frac{1}{nJ}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{u=1}^{J}\xi_{iu}. (110)

Conditional centering immediately gives equation 107.

For two distinct index pairs (i,u)≠(i′,u′)(i,u)\neq(i^{\prime},u^{\prime}), conditional independence and centering imply

𝔼⁡[⟨ξi​u,ξi′​u′⟩ℋZ|ℱn]=0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\langle\xi_{iu},\xi_{i^{\prime}u^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right]=0.

Expanding the squared norm in equation 110 therefore yields

𝔼⁡[‖χ~n,J−χ^n‖ℋZ2|ℱn]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right] =1n2​J2​∑i=1n∑u=1J𝔼⁡[‖ξi​u‖ℋZ2|ℱn]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n^{2}J^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{u=1}^{J}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|\xi_{iu}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{n}\right]
=1n2​J​∑i=1n∫𝒜‖m^n​(a,Xi)−m¯n​(Xi)‖ℋZ2​π​(𝑑a∣Xi)\displaystyle\quad=\frac{1}{n^{2}J}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\left\|\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})-\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i})\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\pi(da\mid X_{i})
=Vnn​J.\displaystyle\quad=\frac{V_{n}}{nJ}.

This proves equation 108. Finally, equation 109 follows by applying conditional Markov’s inequality to

‖χ~n,J−χ^n‖ℋZ2.\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}.

∎

Corollary D.23 (Finite-JJ projected Nyström DR rate).

Suppose the conditions of Corollary D.21 hold, and let (Jn)n≥1(J_{n})_{n\geq 1} be a deterministic sequence of positive integers.

  1. (i)

    Under the bounded-kernel and ridge assumptions already imposed,

    ‖χ~n,Jn−χ^n‖ℋZ=Oℙ​(1n​Jn​λn).\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J_{n}}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{nJ_{n}\lambda_{n}}}\right). (111)

    Consequently,

    ‖χ~n,Jn−χ⁡(π)‖ℋZ\displaystyle\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J_{n}}-\chi(\pi)\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}} =Oℙ(n−1/2+rw,nn−12​(1+γ)+1n​Jn​λn).\displaystyle=O_{\mathbb{P}}\Bigg(n^{-1/2}+r_{w,n}n^{-\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma)}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{nJ_{n}\lambda_{n}}}\Bigg). (112)

    For λn=n−1/(1+γ),\lambda_{n}=n^{-1/(1+\gamma)}, the Monte Carlo term becomes

    1n​Jn​λn=Jn−1/2n−γ2​(1+γ).\frac{1}{\sqrt{nJ_{n}\lambda_{n}}}=J_{n}^{-1/2}n^{-\frac{\gamma}{2(1+\gamma)}}. (113)
  2. (ii)

    If, in addition,

    Vn=Oℙ​(1),V_{n}=O_{\mathbb{P}}(1), (114)

    then

    ‖χ~n,Jn−χ^n‖ℋZ=Oℙ((nJn)−1/2).\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J_{n}}-\widehat{\chi}_{n}\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}\left((nJ_{n})^{-1/2}\right). (115)

    Consequently,

    ‖χ~n,Jn−χ⁡(π)‖ℋZ\displaystyle\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J_{n}}-\chi(\pi)\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}} =Oℙ(n−1/2+rw,nn−12​(1+γ)+(nJn)−1/2).\displaystyle=O_{\mathbb{P}}\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{w,n}n^{-\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma)}}+(nJ_{n})^{-1/2}\right). (116)

    Since Jn≥1J_{n}\geq 1,

    ‖χ~n,Jn−χ(π)‖ℋZ=Oℙ(n−1/2+rw,nn−12​(1+γ)).\left\|\widetilde{\chi}_{n,J_{n}}-\chi(\pi)\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}=O_{\mathbb{P}}\left(n^{-1/2}+r_{w,n}n^{-\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma)}}\right). (117)

    Thus, under equation 114, even a fixed number of target-policy draws per logged context does not change the exact-policy-integral statistical rate.

Proof.

Because the zero operator is feasible in the projected ridge problem, optimality of H^Ln,λn\widehat{H}_{L_{n},\lambda_{n}} gives

λn​‖H^Ln,λn‖HS2\displaystyle\lambda_{n}\left\|\widehat{H}_{L_{n},\lambda_{n}}\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^{2} ≤1n​∑i=1n‖φZ​(Zi)‖ℋZ2≤κZ2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\varphi_{Z}(Z_{i})\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\leq\kappa_{Z}^{2}. (118)

Hence, for every s∈𝒮s\in{\mathcal{S}},

‖m^n​(s)‖ℋZ\displaystyle\left\|\widehat{m}_{n}(s)\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}} =‖H^Ln,λn​φS​(s)‖ℋZ≤‖H^Ln,λn‖HS​‖φS​(s)‖ℋS≤κS​κZλn.\displaystyle=\left\|\widehat{H}_{L_{n},\lambda_{n}}\varphi_{S}(s)\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}\leq\left\|\widehat{H}_{L_{n},\lambda_{n}}\right\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\left\|\varphi_{S}(s)\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{S}}\leq\frac{\kappa_{S}\kappa_{Z}}{\sqrt{\lambda_{n}}}.

Using the Hilbert-space variance identity,

∫𝒜‖m^n​(a,Xi)−m¯n​(Xi)‖ℋZ2​π​(𝑑a∣Xi)≤∫𝒜‖m^n​(a,Xi)‖ℋZ2​π​(𝑑a∣Xi),\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\left\|\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})-\overline{m}_{n}(X_{i})\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\pi(da\mid X_{i})\leq\int_{{\mathcal{A}}}\left\|\widehat{m}_{n}(a,X_{i})\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{Z}}^{2}\pi(da\mid X_{i}),

and therefore

Vn≤κS2​κZ2λn.V_{n}\leq\frac{\kappa_{S}^{2}\kappa_{Z}^{2}}{\lambda_{n}}. (119)

Lemma D.22 now gives equation 111. Combining it with Corollary D.21 and the triangle inequality gives equation 112.

Under equation 114, Lemma D.22 instead gives equation 115. Combining this result with Corollary D.21 gives equation 116. Finally,

(nJn)−1/2≤n−1/2(nJ_{n})^{-1/2}\leq n^{-1/2}

because Jn≥1J_{n}\geq 1, proving equation 117. ∎

Remark D.24 (Choice of the policy Monte Carlo budget).

Under the conservative bound equation 113, a fixed JnJ_{n} still gives a consistent policy-integration approximation because

n​Jn​λn=Jn​nγ1+γ⟶∞.nJ_{n}\lambda_{n}=J_{n}n^{\frac{\gamma}{1+\gamma}}\longrightarrow\infty.

To make the conservative Monte Carlo error no larger than the projected conditional-mean-embedding rate n−1/{2(1+γ)}n^{-1/\{2(1+\gamma)\}}, it is sufficient to choose

Jn≳n1−γ1+γ.J_{n}\gtrsim n^{\frac{1-\gamma}{1+\gamma}}. (120)

Under the stronger variance-tightness condition equation 114, no growth of JnJ_{n} is required to preserve the statistical rate.

D.2 Consistency of the generated particles

Throughout this section, write χ⁡(π)=μQπ\chi(\pi)=\mu_{Q^{\pi}} for the true interventional mean embedding, h^π\widehat{h}_{\pi} for the exact-integral estimator, and h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} for the numerical target used by the particle update. Recall that en,J:=‖h~π−χ⁡(π)‖ℋe_{n,J}:=\|\widetilde{h}_{\pi}-\chi(\pi)\|_{\mathcal{H}} and Q^M(r):=1M​∑j=1MδZj(r)\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)}:=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta_{Z_{j}^{(r)}}.

Throughout this subsection, the particle bounds are understood conditionally on the target-norm event

ℰn:={∥h~π∥ℋ≤κ}.\mathcal{E}_{n}:=\bigl\{\|\widetilde{h}_{\pi}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\kappa\bigr\}.

For h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}, define

sh​(z):=⟨h,φ⁡(z)⟩ℋ,vh​(Q,z)=∇sh​(z)−∫∇1k​(z,z′)​Q​(d​z′).s_{h}(z):=\langle h,\varphi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}},\qquad v_{h}(Q,z)=\nabla s_{h}(z)-\int\nabla_{1}k(z,z^{\prime})\,Q(dz^{\prime}).

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} contain the observations and all target-construction randomness, and let ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r} additionally contain the initial particles and the Gaussian perturbations before iteration rr. The update is

Zj(r+1)=Zj(r)+τvh~π(Q^M(r),Zj(r)+βrUj(r)),j=1,…,M,Z_{j}^{(r+1)}=Z_{j}^{(r)}+\tau v_{\widetilde{h}_{\pi}}\!\left(\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)},Z_{j}^{(r)}+\beta_{r}U_{j}^{(r)}\right),\qquad j=1,\ldots,M,

where, conditional on ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r}, the vectors Uj(r)U_{j}^{(r)} are independent standard Gaussian vectors in ℝdZ\mathbb{R}^{d_{Z}}.

Assumption D.25 (Smooth particle dynamics).

The feature map φ\varphi is twice continuously Fréchet differentiable into ℋ\mathcal{H}. Its norm and the operator norms of its first two derivatives are uniformly bounded by κ≥1\kappa\geq 1. The update uses a constant step size ηr≡τ>0\eta_{r}\equiv\tau>0 and noise levels βr=cβ​(r+1)−α\beta_{r}=c_{\beta}(r+1)^{-\alpha}, where

12​τ​κ2​dZ≤1,0<cβ≤12​dZ,0≤α<12.12\tau\kappa^{2}d_{Z}\leq 1,\qquad 0<c_{\beta}\leq\frac{1}{2\sqrt{d_{Z}}},\qquad 0\leq\alpha<\frac{1}{2}.
Assumption D.26 (Noisy gradient dominance).

For r=0,…,R−1r=0,\ldots,R-1, the particles generated with target h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi} satisfy, almost surely,

1M​∑j=1M𝔼⁡[‖vχ⁡(π)​(Q^M(r),Zj(r)+βr​Uj(r))‖22|ℱr]≥4​κ2​dZ​βr2​MMDk2⁡(Q^M(r),Qπ).\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|v_{\chi(\pi)}\!\left(\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)},Z_{j}^{(r)}+\beta_{r}U_{j}^{(r)}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{r}\right]\geq 4\kappa^{2}d_{Z}\beta_{r}^{2}\operatorname{MMD}_{k}^{2}(\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)},Q^{\pi}).
Lemma D.27 (Descent lemma in expectation).

Under Assumptions D.25 and D.26,

𝔼⁡[‖μQ^M(r+1)−h~π‖ℋ2|ℱr]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\|\mu_{\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r+1)}}-\widetilde{h}_{\pi}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_{r}\right] ≤(1−τ​κ2​dZ8​βr2)​‖μQ^M(r)−h~π‖ℋ2+τ​κ2​(92​dZ​βr2+34)​en,J2.\displaystyle\leq\left(1-\frac{\tau\kappa^{2}d_{Z}}{8}\beta_{r}^{2}\right)\left\|\mu_{\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)}}-\widetilde{h}_{\pi}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}+\tau\kappa^{2}\left(\frac{9}{2}d_{Z}\beta_{r}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}\right)e_{n,J}^{2}.

In particular, with a:=τ​κ2​dZ​cβ28a:=\frac{\tau\kappa^{2}d_{Z}c_{\beta}^{2}}{8}, B:=τ​κ2​(92​dZ​cβ2+34)B:=\tau\kappa^{2}\left(\frac{9}{2}d_{Z}c_{\beta}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}\right), and ar:=a​(r+1)−2​αa_{r}:=a(r+1)^{-2\alpha}, the right-hand side is at most (1−ar)​‖μQ^M(r)−h~π‖ℋ2+B​en,J2(1-a_{r})\left\|\mu_{\widehat{Q}_{M}^{(r)}}-\widetilde{h}_{\pi}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}+Be_{n,J}^{2}.

Under Assumption D.25, for any q>0q>0, conditional on ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r}, with probability at least 1−e−q1-e^{-q},

Remark D.29 (Relation to the stationary MMD points result).

The auxiliary RKHS Lipschitz argument and discrete recursion techniques from the stationary MMD points analysis [9] apply here. Its descent lemma cannot be applied unchanged: the particle update uses h~π\widetilde{h}_{\pi}, whereas the noisy gradient-dominance assumption uses the true target QπQ^{\pi}. Their difference contributes the en,J2e_{n,J}^{2} term in Lemma D.27. The concentration step is stated for the updated particles in Lemma D.28. Solving the squared recursion before taking a square root gives a propagated target error of order Rα​en,JR^{\alpha}e_{n,J} and a finite-particle error of order Rα​log⁡(R/δ)/MR^{\alpha}\sqrt{\log(R/\delta)/M}.

D.3 Numerical-target rate and consistency

Proof of Proposition 5.5.

Apply the exact expansion equation 95 to the exact-integral estimator. Its oracle term is Op(n−1/2)O_{p}(n^{-1/2}) by the finite second moment, its empirical remainder has that order by Assumption 5.4, and its product remainder is Op​(rm,n​rw,n)O_{p}(r_{m,n}r_{w,n}). Conditional on the logged data, landmarks, and fitted nuisances, Lemma D.22 gives mean-square error Vn/(n​J)V_{n}/(nJ) for h~π−h^π\widetilde{h}_{\pi}-\widehat{h}_{\pi}. Conditional Markov’s inequality and Vn=Op​(1)V_{n}=O_{p}(1) imply ∥h~π−h^π∥ℋ=Op((nJ)−1/2)\|\widetilde{h}_{\pi}-\widehat{h}_{\pi}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}}=O_{p}((nJ)^{-1/2}). The triangle inequality proves the claim. This last argument applies to the same fitted regression in both targets, with no additional numerical or subspace discrepancy. ∎

D.4 Outcome-space transfer through the frozen encoder–decoder

We now prove Proposition 5.7 to isolate the error induced by the mapping of the structured outcomes into the encoder’s latent space.

Proof of Proposition 5.7.

First, kEk_{E} is positive definite. Indeed, for arbitrary m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, points y1,…,ym∈𝒴y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\in{\mathcal{Y}}, and coefficients c1,…,cm∈ℝc_{1},\ldots,c_{m}\in\mathbb{R},

Thus, y↦φ⁡(E⁡(y))y\mapsto\varphi(E(y)) is a feature map of kEk_{E}.

Let Q1,Q2Q_{1},Q_{2} be probability laws on 𝒵{\mathcal{Z}} satisfying 𝔼Z∼Qj​‖E⁡(D⁡(Z))−Z‖2<∞\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{j}}\|E(D(Z))-Z\|_{2}<\infty, j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\} Set T=E∘DT=E\circ D. For j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}, define

The definition of a pushforward measure implies that, for every integrable function ff, ∫f⁡(u)​(T#​Qj)​(𝑑u)=∫f⁡(T⁡(z))​Qj​(𝑑z)\int f(u)\,(T_{\#}Q_{j})(du)=\int f(T(z))\,Q_{j}(dz). Applying this identity to the feature map gives

=MMDk⁡(T#​Q1,T#​Q2).\displaystyle=\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(T_{\#}Q_{1},T_{\#}Q_{2}). (123)

This is an exact identity, not an inequality.

Insert and subtract μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2}:

μ~1−μ~2=(μ1−μ2)+(μ~1−μ1)−(μ~2−μ2).\widetilde{\mu}_{1}-\widetilde{\mu}_{2}=(\mu_{1}-\mu_{2})+(\widetilde{\mu}_{1}-\mu_{1})-(\widetilde{\mu}_{2}-\mu_{2}).

The triangle inequality in ℋk{\mathcal{H}}_{k} therefore yields

‖μ~1−μ~2‖ℋk\displaystyle\|\widetilde{\mu}_{1}-\widetilde{\mu}_{2}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}} ≤‖μ1−μ2‖ℋk+∑j=12‖μ~j−μj‖ℋk\displaystyle\leq\|\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}}+\sum_{j=1}^{2}\|\widetilde{\mu}_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}}
=MMDk⁡(Q1,Q2)+∑j=12‖μ~j−μj‖ℋk.\displaystyle=\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(Q_{1},Q_{2})+\sum_{j=1}^{2}\|\widetilde{\mu}_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}}. (124)

For each jj, linearity of the Bochner integral gives

μ~j−μj=𝔼Z∼Qj​[φ⁡(T⁡(Z))−φ⁡(Z)].\widetilde{\mu}_{j}-\mu_{j}=\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{j}}[\varphi(T(Z))-\varphi(Z)].

The norm of a Bochner integral is at most the integral of the norm. Hence,

‖μ~j−μj‖ℋk\displaystyle\|\widetilde{\mu}_{j}-\mu_{j}\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}} ≤𝔼Z∼Qj​‖φ⁡(T⁡(Z))−φ⁡(Z)‖ℋk\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{j}}\|\varphi(T(Z))-\varphi(Z)\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}}
≤Lk​𝔼Z∼Qj​‖T⁡(Z)−Z‖2\displaystyle\leq L_{k}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{j}}\|T(Z)-Z\|_{2}
=Lk​𝔼Z∼Qj​‖E⁡(D⁡(Z))−Z‖2,\displaystyle=L_{k}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{j}}\|E(D(Z))-Z\|_{2}, (125)

where the second inequality is precisely the assumed Lipschitz continuity of the canonical feature map. Combining Equations 123–125 proves

MMDkE⁡(D#​Q1,D#​Q2)≤MMDk⁡(Q1,Q2)+Lk​∑j=12𝔼Z∼Qj​‖E⁡(D⁡(Z))−Z‖2.\displaystyle\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{E}}(D_{\#}Q_{1},D_{\#}Q_{2})\leq\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(Q_{1},Q_{2})+L_{k}\sum_{j=1}^{2}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{j}}\|E(D(Z))-Z\|_{2}. (126)

It remains to prove the claim involving the actual interventional law. Because Qπ=E#​PπQ_{\pi}=E_{\#}P_{\pi}, another application of pushforward integration gives

MMDkE⁡(D#​Q^,Pπ)\displaystyle\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{E}}(D_{\#}\widehat{Q},P_{\pi}) =‖𝔼Z∼Q^​[φ⁡(T⁡(Z))]−𝔼Y∼Pπ​[φ⁡(E⁡(Y))]‖ℋk=‖𝔼Z∼Q^​[φ⁡(T⁡(Z))]−𝔼Z∼Qπ​[φ⁡(Z)]‖ℋk\displaystyle=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\widehat{Q}}[\varphi(T(Z))]-\mathbb{E}_{Y\sim P_{\pi}}[\varphi(E(Y))]\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}}=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\widehat{Q}}[\varphi(T(Z))]-\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim Q_{\pi}}[\varphi(Z)]\right\|_{{\mathcal{H}}_{k}}
=MMDk⁡(T#​Q^,Qπ).\displaystyle=\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(T_{\#}\widehat{Q},Q_{\pi}).

Insert and subtract 𝔼Z∼Q^​[φ​(Z)]\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\widehat{Q}}[\varphi(Z)]. The triangle inequality and equation 125, now with Qj=Q^Q_{j}=\widehat{Q}, give

MMDkE⁡(D#​Q^,Pπ)\displaystyle\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{E}}(D_{\#}\widehat{Q},P_{\pi}) ≤MMDk⁡(Q^,Qπ)+Lk​𝔼Z∼Q^​‖E⁡(D⁡(Z))−Z‖2.\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{MMD}_{k}(\widehat{Q},Q_{\pi})+L_{k}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\widehat{Q}}\|E(D(Z))-Z\|_{2}.

This proves the claim.

∎

Appendix E Supplementary on Numerical Experiments

We first recall the RKHS objects and kernels used by IMMD-Flow. We then give the exact objective, normalization, optimizer, and learning-rate schedules used in our experiments.

E.1 RKHS and Kernels

Let UU take values in a measurable space 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and let k𝒰:𝒰×𝒰→ℝk_{\mathcal{U}}:\mathcal{U}\times\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R} be a measurable positive-definite kernel with RKHS ℋ𝒰\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}}. Its canonical feature map is φ𝒰​(u)=k𝒰​(u,⋅)\varphi_{\mathcal{U}}(u)=k_{\mathcal{U}}(u,\cdot), and the reproducing property gives f⁡(u)=⟨f,φ𝒰​(u)⟩ℋ𝒰f(u)=\langle f,\varphi_{\mathcal{U}}(u)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}}} for every f∈ℋ𝒰f\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}} [6, 22]. If 𝔼⁡[k𝒰​(U,U)]<∞\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{k_{\mathcal{U}}(U,U)}]<\infty, the kernel mean embedding of a law PP is the Bochner expectation

μP:=𝔼U∼P​[φ𝒰​(U)]∈ℋ𝒰,𝔼U∼P​[f⁡(U)]=⟨f,μP⟩ℋ𝒰.\mu_{P}:=\mathbb{E}_{U\sim P}\!\left[\varphi_{\mathcal{U}}(U)\right]\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{U\sim P}[f(U)]=\langle f,\mu_{P}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}}}.

For two laws P,QP,Q, their maximum mean discrepancy is

MMDk𝒰⁡(P,Q):=‖μP−μQ‖ℋ𝒰.\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{\mathcal{U}}}(P,Q):=\|\mu_{P}-\mu_{Q}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}}}.

A characteristic kernel makes P↦μPP\mapsto\mu_{P} injective, in which case zero MMD implies P=QP=Q [56]. Likewise, whenever the conditional Bochner expectation exists,

mU|V​(v):=𝔼⁡[φ𝒰​(U)∣V=v]∈ℋ𝒰m_{U\mid V}(v):=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{\mathcal{U}}(U)\mid V=v]\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{U}}

is the conditional mean embedding of PU|V=vP_{U\mid V=v} [57, 23, 32]. In our construction, U=Z=E⁡(Y)U=Z=E(Y), V=S=(A,X)V=S=(A,X), and mU|Vm_{U\mid V} is the nuisance embedding m0m_{0}. We suppress space and kernel subscripts when they are clear.

Kernels.

For z,z′∈ℝdZz,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{Z}}, we use the radial basis function (RBF) and inverse multiquadric (IMQ) kernels

kRBF​(z,z′,ℓ)\displaystyle k_{\mathrm{RBF}}(z,z^{\prime};\ell) =exp⁡(−‖z−z′‖222​ℓ2),ℓ>0,\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}}{2\ell^{2}}\right),\qquad\ell>0,
kIMQ​(z,z′,c,β)\displaystyle k_{\mathrm{IMQ}}(z,z^{\prime};c,\beta) =(c2+‖z−z′‖22)β,c>0,β<0.\displaystyle=\left(c^{2}+\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}\right)^{\beta},\qquad c>0,\quad\beta<0.

Both are positive-definite kernels. For the Riesz interaction, define

ρs​(z,z′):=‖z−z′‖2s,κs​(z,z′):=−ρs​(z,z′),0<s<2.\rho_{s}(z,z^{\prime}):=\|z-z^{\prime}\|_{2}^{s},\qquad\kappa_{s}(z,z^{\prime}):=-\rho_{s}(z,z^{\prime}),\qquad 0<s<2.

The function κs\kappa_{s} is conditionally positive definite rather than positive definite: for arbitrary points z1,…,zNz_{1},\ldots,z_{N} and coefficients c1,…,cNc_{1},\ldots,c_{N} satisfying ∑a=1Nca=0\sum_{a=1}^{N}c_{a}=0,

∑a=1N∑b=1Nca​cb​κs​(za,zb)≥0.\sum_{a=1}^{N}\sum_{b=1}^{N}c_{a}c_{b}\,\kappa_{s}(z_{a},z_{b})\geq 0.

For any anchor z⋆z_{\star}, the associated anchored kernel

ks,z⋆​(z,z′):=12​{ρs​(z,z⋆)+ρs​(z′,z⋆)−ρs​(z,z′)}k_{s,z_{\star}}(z,z^{\prime}):=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\rho_{s}(z,z_{\star})+\rho_{s}(z^{\prime},z_{\star})-\rho_{s}(z,z^{\prime})\right\}

is positive definite. If X,X′​∼iid​PX,X^{\prime}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}P and Y,Y′​∼iid​QY,Y^{\prime}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}Q, with the required finite ssth moments, then

𝒟s​(P,Q)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{s}(P,Q) :=2​𝔼​ρs​(X,Y)−𝔼​ρs​(X,X′)−𝔼​ρs​(Y,Y′)=2​MMDks,z⋆2⁡(P,Q).\displaystyle:=2\mathbb{E}\rho_{s}(X,Y)-\mathbb{E}\rho_{s}(X,X^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}\rho_{s}(Y,Y^{\prime})=2\,\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{s,z_{\star}}}^{2}(P,Q).

The anchor cancels from this discrepancy. Thus, following the Riesz flow literature, we use a Riesz kernel for the conditionally positive-definite interaction κs\kappa_{s}, while its probability-law discrepancy is equivalently an MMD for the anchored kernel [25, 24].

E.2 Riesz Particle Optimization with AdamW and Warm-up Learning Rate

All reported Riesz experiments use s=1s=1 and the full-dimensional interaction. To distinguish the moving particles from the fixed logged support, write G1,…,GM∈ℝdZG_{1},\ldots,G_{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{Z}} for the equal-mass particles and Z¯i\bar{Z}_{i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, for the fixed target locations in the coordinates supplied to the optimizer. For CelebA and dSprites, the flow coordinates are standardized encodings,

Z¯i={E⁡(Yi)−μ^Z}⊘σ^Z,\bar{Z}_{i}=\{E(Y_{i})-\widehat{\mu}_{Z}\}\oslash\widehat{\sigma}_{Z},

where μ^Z\widehat{\mu}_{Z} and σ^Z\widehat{\sigma}_{Z} are the coordinatewise mean and standard deviation of the logged latents, with standard deviations floored at 10−310^{-3}, and ⊘\oslash denotes coordinatewise division. We apply the inverse affine map before decoding the final particles. The coefficients vi=vDR,iv_{i}=v_{{\rm DR},i} are constructed as in Appendix B. The complete weighted empirical energy is

𝒟s(G1:M;v,Z¯1:n)=\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{s}(G_{1:M};v,\bar{Z}_{1:n})={} 2M​∑j=1M∑i=1nvi​‖Gj−Z¯i‖2s−1M2​∑j=1M∑ℓ=1M‖Gj−Gℓ‖2s−∑i=1n∑q=1nvi​vq​‖Z¯i−Z¯q‖2s.\displaystyle\frac{2}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\|G_{j}-\bar{Z}_{i}\|_{2}^{s}-\frac{1}{M^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\|G_{j}-G_{\ell}\|_{2}^{s}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{q=1}^{n}v_{i}v_{q}\|\bar{Z}_{i}-\bar{Z}_{q}\|_{2}^{s}. (127)

The last term depends only on the fixed target. We therefore optimize

ℒs(G1:M)=2M∑j=1M∑i=1nvi∥Gj−Z¯i∥2s−1M2∑j=1M∑ℓ=1M∥Gj−Gℓ∥2s.\mathcal{L}_{s}(G_{1:M})=\frac{2}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\|G_{j}-\bar{Z}_{i}\|_{2}^{s}-\frac{1}{M^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\|G_{j}-G_{\ell}\|_{2}^{s}. (128)

The first term couples the particles to the fixed weighted target, whereas the second induces repulsion among particles. When vi≥0v_{i}\geq 0 and ∑ivi=1\sum_{i}v_{i}=1, this objective differs from the empirical energy distance only by a target-dependent constant. For generally signed coefficients, we interpret equation 128 as a signed Riesz interaction objective rather than as a discrepancy between two probability laws.

Adaptive scale and particle gradient.

At iteration rr, define

(U1(r),…,UM+n(r)):=(G1(r),…,GM(r),Z¯1,…,Z¯n)(U_{1}^{(r)},\ldots,U_{M+n}^{(r)}):=(G_{1}^{(r)},\ldots,G_{M}^{(r)},\bar{Z}_{1},\ldots,\bar{Z}_{n})

and compute

ar:=max⁡{10−3,1M⁡(M+n)​dZ​∑j=1M∑q=1M+n‖Gj(r)−Uq(r)‖2}.a_{r}:=\max\!\left\{10^{-3},\frac{1}{M(M+n)\sqrt{d_{Z}}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{q=1}^{M+n}\|G_{j}^{(r)}-U_{q}^{(r)}\|_{2}\right\}. (129)

Both the particles and target are divided by ara_{r} before evaluating the loss. The scale is recomputed at each iteration but is treated as constant during differentiation. Consequently, for s=1s=1, the particle gradient is

gj(r)=1ar​{2M​∑i=1nvi​ψ​(Gj(r)−Z¯i)−2M2​∑ℓ=1Mψ⁡(Gj(r)−Gℓ(r))},g_{j}^{(r)}=\frac{1}{a_{r}}\left\{\frac{2}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}\psi(G_{j}^{(r)}-\bar{Z}_{i})-\frac{2}{M^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\psi(G_{j}^{(r)}-G_{\ell}^{(r)})\right\}, (130)

where ψ⁡(u)=u/‖u‖2\psi(u)=u/\|u\|_{2} for u≠0u\neq 0 and ψ⁡(0)=0\psi(0)=0. The implementation uses unsmoothed pairwise Euclidean distances. Thus, a coincident pair contributes the zero subgradient selected by automatic differentiation.

Optimizer and learning-rate schedule.

We optimize the particle locations using AdamW [31, 37], with zero weight decay, ϵA=10−8\epsilon_{\rm A}=10^{-8}, and AMSGrad disabled. The benchmark-specific momentum parameters are reported in Table 4.

Let ηmin=10−6\eta_{\min}=10^{-6}, let ηmax\eta_{\max} denote the peak learning rate, let WW be the number of warm-up iterations, and let RR be the total iteration budget. During warm-up,

ηr=ηmin+(ηmax−ηmin)​rW,0≤r<W.\eta_{r}=\eta_{\min}+\left(\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min}\right)\frac{r}{W},\qquad 0\leq r<W. (131)

After warm-up, we set

ηr=ηmax​ωr,W≤r<R,\eta_{r}=\eta_{\max}\,\omega_{r},\qquad W\leq r<R, (132)

where

ωr={1,constant schedule,12​[1+cos⁡(π​r−WR−W)],cosine schedule.\omega_{r}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{constant schedule},\\[3.0pt] \dfrac{1}{2}\left[1+\cos\!\left(\pi\dfrac{r-W}{R-W}\right)\right],&\text{cosine schedule}.\end{cases} (133)

The algorithm performs exactly RR updates, with no early stopping. The particles are decoded after the final update. A dense iteration costs O⁡(M⁡(n+M)​dZ)O\!\left(M(n+M)d_{Z}\right) time and stores O⁡(M⁡(n+M))O\!\left(M(n+M)\right) pairwise distances.

E.3 Details on Data-Generating Processes

We evaluate IMMD-Flow on three main benchmarks. ColorMNIST and CelebA evaluate structured image outcomes under discrete interventions and are adapted from Dance et al. [15]. dSprites evaluates a stochastic intervention with a continuous action and is adapted from the setting of Zenati et al. [62]. We additionally use a two-dimensional null-effect mixture Dance et al. [15] in our ablation studies (see Appendix E.6). We describe the exact constructions used in our experiments below.

ColorMNIST.

We adapt the foreground-color confounding benchmark of Dance et al. [15] that uses MNIST images [33]. We generate

X\displaystyle X ∼Unif⁡[0,1],\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1],
A|X=x\displaystyle A\mid X=x ∼Bernoulli⁡(σℓ​(w⁡(x−1/2))),\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma_{\ell}\!\left(w(x-1/2)\right)\right),
S|A=a\displaystyle S\mid A=a ∼P^da,(d0,d1)=(1,6).\displaystyle\sim\widehat{P}_{d_{a}},\quad(d_{0},d_{1})=(1,6).

Here, P^da\widehat{P}_{d_{a}} is the uniform empirical law of grayscale MNIST training images with label dad_{a}; images are sampled with replacement. For S∈[0,1]28×28S\in[0,1]^{28\times 28}, define

M⁡(S)\displaystyle M(S) =σℓ​(κ⁡(S−τ)),cfg​(x)=(x,α,1−x)⊤,Y=M⁡(S)⊙(cfg​(X)⊗S).\displaystyle=\sigma_{\ell}\!\left(\kappa(S-\tau)\right),\kern 5.0ptc_{\mathrm{fg}}(x)=(x,\alpha,1-x)^{\top},\kern 5.0ptY=M(S)\odot\bigl(c_{\mathrm{fg}}(X)\otimes S\bigr).

The sigmoid and mask operations are pixelwise, and the background is black. Our default configuration uses (w,κ,τ,α)=(10,20,0.08,0.2)(w,\kappa,\tau,\alpha)=(10,20,0.08,0.2). The confounding ablation varies w∈{1,…,10}w\in\{1,\ldots,10\}. To sample from PY⁡(a)P_{Y(a)}, we fix the digit class at dad_{a}, independently redraw X∼Unif⁡[0,1]X\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], and draw another image from P^da\widehat{P}_{d_{a}}.

CelebA.

This benchmark evaluates population-level hair-color standardization within each sex group. We use the CelebA data set [35] and follow the controlled construction of Dance et al. [15]. Let

A=𝟏​{Male},X=𝟏​{Blond​Hair}.A=\bm{1}\{\mathrm{Male}\},\qquad X=\bm{1}\{\mathrm{Blond\ Hair}\}.

We combine the official training and validation splits, retain images with exactly one of the blond-hair and brown-hair labels, and exclude images labeled black hair, gray hair, bald, or wearing a hat. Let P^a,x\widehat{P}_{a,x} denote the empirical image distribution in cell (A=a,X=x)(A=a,X=x).

The logged design is

Pobs​(X=1)\displaystyle P_{\mathrm{obs}}(X=1) =q=0.3,Pobs(A=1∣X=0)=0.6,Pobs(A=1∣X=1)=0.1,Y∣(A=a,X=x)∼P^a,x.\displaystyle=q=0.3,\quad P_{\mathrm{obs}}(A=1\mid X=0)=0.6,\quad P_{\mathrm{obs}}(A=1\mid X=1)=0.1,\quad Y\mid(A=a,X=x)\sim\widehat{P}_{a,x}.

Conditional on each cell, images are sampled without replacement. Let na​x=#{i:Ai=a,Xi=x}n_{ax}=\#\{i:A_{i}=a,X_{i}=x\}. At nobs=20,000n_{\mathrm{obs}}=20{,}000, the counts (n00,n01,n10,n11)(n_{00},n_{01},n_{10},n_{11}) are (5,600,5,400,8,400,600)(5{,}600,5{,}400,8{,}400,600). For each sex group aa, the target standardizes the hair-color composition to

Pa⋆=(1−q)​P^a,0+q​P^a,1.\displaystyle P_{a}^{\star}=(1-q)\widehat{P}_{a,0}+q\widehat{P}_{a,1}.

We use 2,0002{,}000 held-out reference images per group: 1,4001{,}400 brown-haired and 600600 blond-haired images. Logged and reference images are disjoint within every cell. This is population-level post-stratification within a sex group; it is not a same-person edit or a literal intervention on sex. We center-crop the aligned images to 178×178178\times 178, resize them to 256×256256\times 256, and scale pixels to [−1,1][-1,1].

dSprites.

We construct a confounded continuous-action benchmark from dSprites [42], extending the setup of Zenati et al. [62]. Draw X=(X1,X2)∼Unif⁡([0,1]2)X=(X_{1},X_{2})\sim\mathrm{Unif}([0,1]^{2}) and set

C⁡(X)\displaystyle C(X) =min⁡{2,⌊3​X1⌋},\displaystyle=\min\{2,\lfloor 3X_{1}\rfloor\}, S⁡(X)\displaystyle S(X) =min⁡{5,⌊6​X2⌋},\displaystyle=\min\{5,\lfloor 6X_{2}\rfloor\},

which select one of three shapes and six scales; orientation is fixed at zero. Let RθR_{\theta} denote the two-dimensional rotation matrix and define μ0​(x)=1.8​Rπ/6​(x−12​𝟏2)\mu_{0}(x)=1.8R_{\pi/6}(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{1}_{2}). The logging and target policies are

π0(⋅∣x)\displaystyle\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid x) =𝒩⁡(μ0​(x),0.62​I2),\displaystyle={\mathcal{N}}\!\left(\mu_{0}(x),0.6^{2}I_{2}\right),
π(⋅∣x)\displaystyle\pi(\cdot\mid x) =12​𝒩​(μ0​(x),0.62​I2)+12​𝒩​(μ0​(x)+Δ,0.62​I2),Δ=(0.45,−0.45)⊤.\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}{\mathcal{N}}\!\left(\mu_{0}(x),0.6^{2}I_{2}\right)+\tfrac{1}{2}{\mathcal{N}}\!\left(\mu_{0}(x)+\Delta,0.6^{2}I_{2}\right),\qquad\Delta=(0.45,-0.45)^{\top}.

The corresponding oracle importance ratio is

π⁡(a∣x)π0​(a∣x)=12+12​exp⁡{Δ⊤​(a−μ0​(x))0.62−∥Δ∥222​(0.62)}.\displaystyle\frac{\pi(a\mid x)}{\pi_{0}(a\mid x)}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\exp\!\left\{\frac{\Delta^{\top}(a-\mu_{0}(x))}{0.6^{2}}-\frac{\lVert\Delta\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2(0.6^{2})}\right\}.

For j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}, the continuous image coordinate is pj​(a)=31​σℓ​(1.5​aj)p_{j}(a)=31\sigma_{\ell}(1.5a_{j}). The deterministic outcome Y=g⁡(X,A)∈[0,1]64×64Y=g(X,A)\in[0,1]^{64\times 64} is obtained by bilinearly interpolating the four neighboring dSprites templates at p⁡(A)p(A), using the shape and scale selected by XX; no pixel noise is added. Thus XX affects both treatment and visual content, whereas AA controls position, so adjustment for the backdoor path A←X→YA\leftarrow X\rightarrow Y is necessary. The policy changes the coupling between content and position while preserving the marginal distribution of shape and scale. Fresh draws X⋆∼PXX^{\star}\sim P_{X}, A⋆∼π(⋅∣X⋆)A^{\star}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid X^{\star}), and Y⋆=g⁡(X⋆,A⋆)Y^{\star}=g(X^{\star},A^{\star}) provide exact oracle target samples.

Two-dimensional Gaussian mixture.

We use the null-effect deconfounding benchmark of Dance et al. [15]. Define σℓ​(t)=(1+e−t)−1\sigma_{\ell}(t)=(1+e^{-t})^{-1} and b=(1,−1)⊤/2b=(1,-1)^{\top}/\sqrt{2}. We generate

X\displaystyle X ∼𝒩(0,I2),A∣X=x∼Bernoulli(σℓ(γb⊤x)),\displaystyle\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,I_{2}),\quad A\mid X=x\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma_{\ell}(\gamma b^{\top}x)\right),
B\displaystyle B ∼Bernoulli⁡(1/2),ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σY2​I2),Y=X+δ​B​𝟏2+ϵ.\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2),\quad\epsilon\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma_{Y}^{2}I_{2}),\quad Y=X+\delta B\bm{1}_{2}+\epsilon.

Here, BB and ϵ\epsilon are mutually independent and independent of (X,A)(X,A). We set (γ,δ,σY)=(3,2,0.2)(\gamma,\delta,\sigma_{Y})=(3,2,0.2). Treatment does not enter the outcome equation. Hence PY⁡(0)=PY⁡(1)=PYP_{Y(0)}=P_{Y(1)}=P_{Y}, although PY|A=aP_{Y\mid A=a} generally differs from PYP_{Y}.

E.4 Autoencoders for Image Experiments

For ColorMNIST and dSprites, we train convolutional autoencoders on all logged images once per experimental repetition and freeze them before constructing the target embedding and running the particle flow. The ColorMNIST encoder maps a 3×28×283\times 28\times 28 input through three stride-two convolutional blocks with 3232, 6464, and 128128 channels and spatial sizes 1414, 77, and 44, respectively. Each block uses group normalization and a SiLU activation, and a linear layer produces a 32-dimensional bottleneck. Its mirrored transposed-convolution decoder ends with a tanh output. The dSprites encoder maps a 1×64×641\times 64\times 64 input through four analogous blocks with 3232, 6464, 128128, and 128128 channels and spatial sizes 3232, 1616, 88, and 44, followed by a 32-dimensional bottleneck; its mirrored decoder ends with a sigmoid output. We minimize reconstruction MSE using Adam [31], with batch size 128128 and learning rate 10−310^{-3}, for 3,0003{,}000 ColorMNIST iterations and 4,0004{,}000 dSprites iterations. During dSprites training, we add fresh Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.050.05 to each input and reconstruct the corresponding logged image. The statistical analysis in Section 5 treats EE and DD as fixed independently of the estimation sample. The same-sample autoencoder training used for ColorMNIST and dSprites in our experiments is not covered by the present guarantees.

For CelebA, we instead use the frozen pretrained stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-mse VAE [49], without fine-tuning, and encode each 256×256256\times 256 image by the posterior mode into a 4×32×324\times 32\times 32 latent. In every case, IMMD-Flow operates on the fixed latent representations and the final particles are decoded to image space.

E.5 Qualitative samples and particle evolution

In this section, we present qualitative examples of the initialized and generated particles. We also visualize selected particles at intermediate iterations to illustrate how the empirical distribution evolves under the fixed estimated target.

ColorMNIST samples.

For an image yy, let R⁡(y)R(y) and B⁡(y)B(y) denote its total red- and blue-channel intensities, and define the foreground-colour statistic

c⁡(y):=R⁡(y)R⁡(y)+B⁡(y).c(y):=\frac{R(y)}{R(y)+B(y)}. (134)

Values near zero correspond to predominantly blue foregrounds, values near one correspond to predominantly red foregrounds, and c⁡(y)=1/2c(y)=1/2 represents equal red and blue content. Under the ColorMNIST renderer, c⁡(Y)=Xc(Y)=X up to reconstruction and numerical error, because the red and blue foreground intensities are proportional to XX and 1−X1-X, respectively. Since the intervention preserves X∼Unif⁡[0,1]X\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], the oracle mean of this statistic is 1/21/2.

Figure 3 compares particles before and after IMMD-Flow in both intervention arms. The initialized observational-arm particles have foreground-colour distributions shifted in opposite directions. The final particles move toward the interventional colour law while largely preserving the treatment-specific digit identity.

CelebA samples.

Figure 4 presents initialized and final particles for both sex groups. The generated particles remain visually coherent while changing under the fixed population-level hair-colour target.

Particle evolution on CelebA.

Figure 5 shows selected particles at intermediate iterations. The decoded images change gradually rather than being replaced by unrelated samples, while the target embedding and its coefficients remain fixed throughout optimization.

E.6 Additional experiments and ablations

We complement the main benchmark comparisons with a low-dimensional illustration and a series of ablations examining the effects of the logged sample size, particle count, particle initialization, projected Nyström approximation, and confounding strength. Unless an experiment varies the stated component, we use the doubly robust target, full-sample nuisance fitting, projected Nyström regression, observed-outcome initialization, and M=2,000M=2{,}000 particles. ColorMNIST uses the IMQ–Euler update, while CelebA and dSprites use Riesz–AdamW. For the two-dimensional benchmark, we report both RBF–Euler and Riesz–AdamW.

Entries are means and sample standard deviations across three data seeds. For the two static interventions, metrics are first averaged across intervention arms within each seed. For dSprites, they are averaged across ten fresh target-policy draws within each seed. Outcome- and latent-space SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} values are multiplied by 10310^{3} throughout this subsection.

Null-effect deconfounding illustration.

We first illustrate IMMD-Flow on the two-dimensional null-effect benchmark of Dance et al. [15] which is explained in the previous section. Treatment does not enter the outcome equation, so

PY⁡(0)=PY⁡(1)=PY.P_{Y(0)}=P_{Y(1)}=P_{Y}.

Nevertheless, treatment assignment depends on XX, which also enters the outcome equation. Consequently, the observational arm distributions PY|A=aP_{Y\mid A=a} generally differ from the common interventional law PYP_{Y}.

Figure 6 compares particles initialized from each observational arm with the particles returned by DR–IMMD. The initial clouds overrepresent different regions of the common target, whereas the flowed particles recover its overall mixture structure more accurately. Figure 7 visualizes representative particle paths during optimization.

The trajectories are generally curved because each particle follows a time-varying MMD witness determined by the evolving empirical particle distribution. They are not intended to approximate straight optimal-transport displacement paths.

Effect of the logged sample size.

Table 5 shows that IMMD-Flow substantially reduces outcome-space and, where applicable, latent-space SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} relative to initialization at every sample size. The final discrepancies generally improve as nn increases on the structured-outcome benchmarks, most clearly for CelebA and dSprites, whereas the two-dimensional results fluctuate within their across-seed variability. FID behaves differently across benchmarks: the flow improves it on ColorMNIST, changes it little on dSprites, and slightly increases it on CelebA.

Effect of the particle count.

Table 6 shows that increasing MM consistently reduces the final outcome- and latent-space SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} across all benchmarks. Relative to the same particles before optimization, IMMD-Flow gives substantial improvements throughout the two-dimensional, ColorMNIST, and dSprites experiments. On CelebA, small particle clouds remain inaccurate in outcome space, but the flow improves upon initialization from M=500M=500 onward, with increasingly clear gains as MM grows.

The final FID also decreases with MM. However, because FID is estimated from MM generated images against a fixed reference set, part of this trend reflects its finite-sample dependence. We therefore use FID primarily for initial-versus-flow comparisons at a fixed particle count, rather than to quantify the effect of MM in isolation.

Effect of particle initialization.

We examine the sensitivity of IMMD-Flow to its initial particle distribution. We compare initialization from observed outcomes with Gaussian alternatives of increasing distance from the observed outcome geometry. The moment-matched Gaussian uses the empirical mean and full covariance. For CelebA, the standardized normal is 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I) in the standardized flow coordinates and therefore matches the empirical coordinatewise location and scale, while the raw-encoder normal draws 𝒩⁡(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I) before applying the standardization map. All other target-estimation and optimization settings are held fixed.

Observed-outcome initialization gives the strongest results on ColorMNIST and CelebA, indicating that starting on the learned image manifold can materially facilitate particle optimization. On CelebA, the full moment-matched Gaussian attains almost the same latent SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} as the observed initialization, but substantially worse outcome-space SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} and FID. Thus, matching low-order latent moments does not by itself ensure realistic decoded samples.

In the two-dimensional benchmark, the preferred initialization depends on the particle update, while dSprites is nearly insensitive to the three initializations considered. Overall, observational initialization is most beneficial for the more complex image distributions, rather than being uniformly optimal.

Full ridge versus projected Nyström.

We compare the full-ridge and projected-Nyström constructions of the conditional mean embedding on ColorMNIST. The paired runs use the same data seeds, intervention arms, and particle-flow settings. The projected estimator uses mL=1024m_{L}=1024 uniformly sampled landmarks. Table 8 reports the resulting outcome-space discrepancy and the wall-clock time required to solve the conditional-mean-embedding regression.

The full-ridge solve scales cubically in nn (0.20→1.26→9.090.20\to 1.26\to 9.09 seconds), while the projected Nyström solve is flat at 0.030.03–0.040.04 seconds, a 6.7×6.7\times to 227×227\times reduction over this range, at no cost in outcome-space discrepancy.

Effect of confounding strength.

For ColorMNIST, the parameter ww controls the strength of the association between treatment and the context determining foreground colour. Increasing ww makes the treatment assignment more deterministic and weakens effective overlap. We vary w∈{1,…,10}w\in\{1,\ldots,10\} while holding n=20,000n=20{,}000, M=2,000M=2{,}000, and all remaining settings fixed.

As ww increases, the observational-arm initialization moves progressively farther from the interventional target, with its SW2\mathrm{SW}_{2} increasing from 10.8910.89 to 43.3243.32. In contrast, the final discrepancy remains comparatively stable, increasing only from 7.607.60 to 9.469.46. Thus, DR–IMMD corrects most of the confounding-induced distribution shift throughout the sweep, with only gradual degradation at the strongest assignment levels.

E.7 Compute resources

All experiments were run on an internal SLURM-managed cluster of Linux x86_64 nodes, using Python 3.12.12 with PyTorch 2.10.0 built against CUDA 12.6 (NVIDIA driver 580.95.05). Each run was submitted as a single-node, single-task job requesting one GPU, two to eight CPU cores, between 12 GB and 64 GB of system memory, and a wall-clock limit of four to twelve hours; parameter sweeps were executed as SLURM job arrays with one configuration per array task. The ColorMNIST and dSprites experiments used a single NVIDIA L40S GPU with approximately 46 GB of memory, and the CelebA experiments a single NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB with 40 GB; the two-dimensional synthetic design contains no GPU code and was run on CPU. Every wall-clock comparison we report was pinned to one GPU model, so no timing is compared across hardware.

E.8 Existing assets, licences, and sensitive content

All datasets used in this paper are existing research benchmarks and are used solely for research evaluation. ColorMNIST is derived from MNIST, which is made available under the Creative Commons Attribution--ShareAlike 3.0 Unported (CC BY-SA 3.0) licence. dSprites is obtained from the official Google DeepMind repository11 1 https://github.com/google-deepmind/dsprites-dataset, which is distributed under the Apache License 2.0. CelebA is used under its dataset agreement for non-commercial research purposes only. The supplementary code does not redistribute CelebA; users must obtain the dataset from its official source and comply with its terms of use. For CelebA, we load the pretrained stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-mse checkpoint through the Hugging Face Diffusers implementation of AutoencoderKL.22 2 Diffusers: https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers; model checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-mse. The Diffusers library is distributed under the Apache License 2.0, whereas the model repository lists an MIT licence. We use the model only as a fixed encoder and decoder and do not fine-tune or redistribute its weights. We do not redistribute external datasets or pretrained model weights, and provide only code and instructions for obtaining these assets from their original sources.

CelebA contains identifiable photographs of public figures together with binary appearance annotations, including the dataset’s sex and hair-colour labels. We use CelebA only as a controlled benchmark for population-level distributional rebalancing: we do not perform identity recognition or make person-specific causal claims. The results should not be interpreted as establishing that the generated distributions are demographically representative, fair, or appropriate for real-world use. No new human annotations or participant data were collected.
